div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Mi:haelmas C40099.---The' Cll3toOl of eating goose nn Michaelmas Day is said by one account to have originated from the accidental circumstance that Queen Elizabeth was dining off this bird, when she heard of the victory of Sir Francis Drake, over the Spanish Armada. In gratefal remembrance she afterwards always dined off the goose on Michaelel£l6 D y,and it thus became an English custom. There are,however, other versions of this, and other old Michaelmas customs of which there are many and vaxiona in different parts of the British Isles. It is, however, more than probable that , the Michaelmas geose gained its reputation from the I fact that that was the natural time of year for its arriving at a fit; aad proper stage for the table, and it was a common custom in ancient time; for lords of the manor to receive a goose at ;Michaelmas from their tenants, as part of their rents, and services. Tbere is an old adage that "if you eat goose on hlichaelmas D tv,You I will never want money all the year round" a not unpleasant way, for those who have faith in ancient sayings of providing against financial difficulties, and "the eternal want of peace." _

Lord Burton and Greeguoich.—Lord Burton is under- stood to intend giving Gleneuoich, where he has been entertaining the King for a week's shooting and fiahing. It is one of the finest sporting estates in Scot- land, and of which Lord Burton has held a lease for over:twenty years. The previous tenant was the Duke of Marlborough. who was content with the then modest proportions of the Lodge. Lord Burton greatly enlarged and modernized the mansion, which is now fitted with the electric light, and all the up-to-date improvements. But, the forest of Glenquoich is still as it ever was, the horse of the deer, and is said to yield every year about one hundred of the finest stage in Scotland. These, however, Fire just as wary of Royal sportsmen as of others, and the King appears to have been less fortunate than some of Lord Burton's other guests, in getting within shooting distance of them. The Smartest Hunting Quarters.-llnnting like many other things, is spoken of as having suffered decadence since the "good old times." The hounds are not what they were, railways, barbed wire and the overcrowding of the nouveau riche, are all matters referred to as having marred the best traditions of the sport. But in spite of all this, the hunting field still attracts a great many of the smartest people, and in which it is still the ambition of every girl and fashionable woman to be to the fore. Melton. Oakham, Market Harborough, and all that interesting part of the country known as the " Dukeries," are among the smartest hunting quarters. Welbeck, where the Duke and Duchess of Portland always entertain a succession of hunting parties, is a famous centre, and so also is Clmnber, the residence of the Duke and Duchess of Newcastle. There is also a famous pack of hounds at Belvoir, belonginr to the venerable Duke of Rutland. The hounds of Bel voir own pedigree dating beck to 1750, and the Rennet books, which are much prized by the Duke, have been most carefully kept, from that time down to the preaent oay.

—Ai Ideal Novelist.—By the death of Dr. George Macdonald, English and Scottish literature has lost one of its most gifted contributors, but we may be sure that -having reached the age p f four score years, he was well content to regard his wbrk as finished and to afford as example of the truth of his own lines : Better a death, when work is done Than earth's most favoured birth— Of his works one may say as Lord Lythelton said of Thomson, that he wrote no line whioh, dying, he could wish to blot out, and in these days we can ill-afford to take leave of a poet and novelist, of Dr. Macdonald's ' stamp,without expressing our gratitude for books whose tone was as pure as tho style in which they were written.

Titled Authoresses.—The latest titled recruit to the literary, world is the Duchess of Buckingham who is -shortly-pnblishing a book of fairy tales which have been handed down from generation to generation in her family. It will no doubt prove a desirable acquisition in that somewhat aeglected branch of contemporary literature—stories for children, as they are to be real sold-fashioned fairy tales just as the Duchess heard them when a child. We have thus another addition to the many titled women of literary taste. who already include several of the Duchesses, Countesses, and many others who have been born in the purple. Amongst the best kno.on are the Duchess of Sutherland and the Drichess of Leeds, who, both as writers of fiction and of more serious work, have made a highly successful appeal to the reading public. It is singular, however, that titled authoresses seldom if ever attempt to chew the life they know best. The factory girl delights in nothing so much as a first-rate novel of fashionable life' morals and manners, but those writers who belong to the exclusive world torn their thoughts in other directions, and almost invariably give their story or subject a more plebian setting of common and everyday life. The Art of Shopping.—Unquestionably the American woman can " give us points" in the matter of shopoisg. In the first place she knoffs what she wants, and will take nothing else, despite the assurance of attendants .and shopwalkers, that wkat they happen to have in stock is far preferable in every way. Then she spares be pains to find out the shops which make a speciality of this article or that, and she usually knows where the best fit and the lowest prices are to be obtained. The young Duchess of Roxburghe and Lady Donnoughmore, are both expeditious yet careful shoppers, and many an extravagant thoughtless Society woman would do well to follow in their footsteps. Despite their great wealth the Duchess and Lady Donnoughasore refuse to pay exorbitant prices in the West End for articles they can obtain on more reasonable terms in less fashionable quarters of the town, moreover a rule from which they seldom, if ever deviate, is. an estimate for every order, and little or no credit. The Duchess of Roxbilrghe was, it will be remembered, Miss May Goelet, an American -heiress of many millions. Luxurious Coats.—Long velvet coats are to hive a tremendous vogue, this winter, so say Parisian and Viennese tailors, but, as a matter of fact, only the wealthy woman can afford so luxurons it garment. To the firs,: place velvet is a costly fabric, secondly it has to be worn very carefully, contact with rain, dust and rand, proving disastrous in the extreme, while last, but by no means least,velvet does not take kindly to being sat upon and creased, a procedure to which the tails of a coat must often be subject. A little velvet coatee however, is often within the reach of the moderately endowed especially if such a garment is built at home, is by no means difficult task in these data of simple, and reliabl e patterns. The new velvet, intended eepecially for the building of coats, is extremely supple and soft, finer and softer than the beautiful velours

div.head: IS SUNLIGHT INJURIOUS?
div.p: IS SUNLIGHT INJURIOUS?

Major Charles E. Woodruff, in a work dealing with tropical light on white men, has brought much interesting matter together with a view td showing that excessive light is destructive of energy as well as of complexions, and leads to Jegeueration. Among other arguments in sup- /sort of the case against sunlight it is stated that the vast majority of animals live in darkness, hiding irom the light. A " day animal," we are told, `'exists solely because its opaque armour keeps out the deadly arrows of light." Speak- ing of coloured people, the author says:. 'The shadow'd livery of the burnished sun" is an index of degeneracy.

div.head: TESTING FOR ARSENIC.
div.p: TESTING FOR ARSENIC.

One of the familiar tests by which a chemist recognises the presence of arsenic is the odour of garlic given off when one of its compounds is heated in the blowpipe flame. The same smell of garlic is produced when certain fungi grow on substances containing arsenic. And it is interesting to note that one species of fungus is found to accomplish this feat of chemical analy- sis more . effectively when it is grown in connec- tion with yellow algal cells—in other words, when it forms the plant association known as a lichen. The above method of detecting arsea ic seems specially applicable to cases of poisoning where the substance is mixed with organic, mat- ter which would form a suitable medium for the culture of the fungus.

3IA DGE.
MECHANISM OF
VOLCANIC ERUPTIONS.

The accepted mechanism of a volcanic eruption is, says a distinguished scientist, that 1 molten magma rises in the volcano chinmey. It con- sists of fusible silicates and other more or less re- fractory minerals, sometimes already partly cry- stalfised, and the whole highly charged with water and gases, which are kept in a liquid state by the immense pressure to which they are sub- jected. When the mass rises nearer the surface and the pressure is diminished, the water and gases expand into vapour and blow a certain portion of the heavier and less fusible materials to powder, or, short of this, form pumice stone, which is really solidified froth, and they are vio- lently discharged from the crater. When the greater part of the steam and gases have been discharged, the lava, still rising, gets Vent, either over the lip of the crater or often through a lateral fissure, and flows quietly down the side of the mountain. The mixture of solid particles and incandescent gas behaves like a heavy liquid, and before the solid particles have time to subside, the whole rolls down the side of the mountain under the influence of gravity, and consequently gathers speed and momentum as it goes. The heavy solid particles are gradually deposited, and the remaining steam and gases, thus relieved of their burden, are free to ascend.

FURS AND FASHION GOSSIP.

London furriers are showing a great many beautiful sets of ermine and chinchilla; white fox and silvered fox am also much to the fore. Some of the ermine stoles reach almost to tho feet of the wearers. Starting with a narrow band at the back of the neck, they spread wider and wider until they finish with rounded ends, each of which is nearly 9in. 'wide. The smaller stoles are made in the same style. Almost all the new felt hats have trimmings of velvet. Sometimes velvet ribbon is closely pleated and takes the place of a band round the crown, while a couple of ostrich plumes com- plete the ornamentation. Sometimes a band of velvet edges the brim, or a full cap of velvet covers the crown. Boots and shoes are worn narrower and longer than ever, and even, for the autumn and winter a number are made in the light tones of antelope skin, dark grey, and golden-tan. and many have black feet or brown feet with white or grey uppers.

div.head: SUART CLOTS. COSTIMII.
div.p: SUART CLOTS. COSTIMII.

The original of the trim little costume appear- ing in our present sketch was realised in a fine faced cloth of a bright navy tint. The coat fits tightly, and buttons over with three gradated buttons on the left side, while it opens towards the waist to shew a waistcoat. The coat is finished with turn-down cuffs and collar, which, with the waistcoat, are faced with scarlet cloth. The skirt is a pleated one, earth pleat being

secured by a set of gradated buttons like thosd on the coat; but these pleats are nearly hidden beneath the long basque which is attached to the coat. The longer the basque, the more modish the coat at the present moment; and this is a sensible fashion for winter time, when we need more clothing round the• hips than we often allow ourselves. The felt hat which is worn with this costume has no trimming on top, but has three large quills fixed to the bandeau at tho back.

div.head: BRIDES FROM THE FAR EAST.
div.p: BRIDES FROM THE FAR EAST.

In view of the fact that the Weiltern maid is .hewing more and more disposition towards in- dependence and more and more dislike of maternity, it is prophesied that it may be to- wards the Far East that prospective Western bridegrooms will look for wives in the early future. La belle Americaine's influence, has not always been found altogether beneficial to Eng- lish society; but Yokohama San is a young person with no mind of her own. She is even taught to bo amiable to her mother-in-law, never to be angry with her husband, never to dress too expensively, to be economical in the house- hold, and to regard maternity as her bounden duty. If no English or American woman of this pattern is to be found, and if man wants what he describes as an ideal wife, it is possible that he may contemplate going East for her. Per- sonally, however, remarks " Miranda " in the Lady's Pictorial, I think the day is very remote.

HOW LIGHT CAUSES LEAF MOVEMENTS. It is a matter of common knowledge that plants are sensitive to light. The majority of leaves, for example, possess the , power of placing themselves at right angles to the direc- tion of the light falling on them. In this way they obtain the maximum effect from the light rays which reach them. The means by which this is accomplished, and how the light stimu- lates the leaf to make the necessary movements, however, has not been shown. Dr. G. Haber- landt, Professor of Botany in the University of Graz, contends that the plants have organs which he calls " ocelli," or eyes, through which the ne- cessary movements are accomplished. And if this is so, remarks the Globe, the first question is, on what parts of the plants are these eyes to be found? By experiments in which the blade of the leaf was covered with black paper, Dr. Haborlandt shewed that the principal sensitive- ness must be in the leaf itself, and not in the stalk. However, this programme, as I gathered, pre- sented in operation certain practical difficulties: for the cottage had but two floors, and as Meary Jane bad already made her appearance upon this earthly scene in the upper one, Mole regarded that obstacle as insuperable. " f3he can't goo upstairs," she said, " because there ballet no furder stairs for her to goo up." But Lucy Lockett, calmly confident, waived aside the ob- jection with the conscious superiority of a woman of business—a woman of resources. " Lot I stand on tit* there chair," she suggested, " an' you hand lup the babby. Then been rise in the end, zure enough, von her'll have goo'd up in the world avore ivver !leen goo'd down in it." There was a scuffling of chairs and a peal of laughter. Meary Jane's ad vauce iu life having been 'thus carefully assured, the two women car- ried her down in their arms to Awlfurd, who was sitting just inside the cottage, smoking his afternoon pipe with an unclouded conscience. Awlfurd is a broom squire : therefore he does not trouble himself to work overtime like the bond-slaves of capitalism. On the contrary, be conducts his life with the careless ease of a gen- 'tleman of leisure. I often envy Awlfurd Zum- mere the freedom denied to the mere man of let- ters. I am bound to admit that Awlfurd did not un- necessarily excite himself over the incident of the baby. The duties of paternity sat lightly on his broad shoulders. One more or less matters little to Awlfurd. He does not have to. mend his chil- dren to Eton or Girton. The casual advent of another young Briton had long since ceased to interest him. " Wet do 'ea think o'• the bahby ?" Lucy asked, holding forth to him with just pride. She regarded herself on all such occasions as the authorised show woman. Awlfurd withdrew his pipe from his teeth slowly. His intellect did not move with any ex- cessive speed : he was no mental scorcher. " Nivver mod a viner babby in all my barn days," he responded after a long deep pause, inspecting the poor red-and-white morsel of humanity with critical eyes. Awlfard was used to these events, and know too well to fly in the face of Lucy Lockett'e principles. He thought it better to get over the inevitable avowal at once, and have done with it. " 'E'll have to goo round to Upton Parva an' registrate her to-morrow," Lucy Lockett con- firmed : Lucy was always great on all forms and ceremonies. "Zo you'd better look sharp an' make up your mind wot 'ee mean to call her. If I didn't nutiiko 'cc, 'ee'd goo into the regis- trator's wi'out ivver havin' thought o' it." " I bain't one as holds with thik there regis- trating," Awlfurd remarked, in a pugnacious tone, but with oue eye on his pipe and one on Lucy. "Us did vurry well wi' the old- vashioned

chris'nin", avore ivver the registrating game were invented. Bain't one of 'em enough ? Wet vor do they gurt yolks want to goo an' make we poor nag christen our childer two or three times awver vor ?" " Awlfurd Zummers," Lucy exclaimed, glar-

Not regisirate her, indeed An' this a Chrisebun _

but a greet lazy, hulking, good-vor-tmffin vulla like you 'ould want to goo aside o' it. llows'ever, like it or lump it, its all one. 'Ee've got to do it, wether 'ee wants it or wether 'ee dontet,—zo, that's n blessing. There built% but one thing the law allows 'eta to choose, an' that is the name 'ee's going to registrato her by." " Lizbetles a proper vine name," Awlfurd mused to himself, holding his pipe in his hand and regarding it intently. " Lizbeth was my mother's name, avore she took to drink an' died, an' it's Lizzie's name too. I've allus had a vancy vor that name, Mrs. Lockett. Wy, the yurry vitst gun on thik here hill that I ivver went a. coorthe with, I mind, was Lizbeth." Lucy Lockett held up her hands in dare. eating horror. " Lard, Awlfurd, her can't be Lizbeth now," she cried.. " 'Ee mustn't say the name out avore ohrimemmned. If 'ee do want to call her Lizbeth, 'ee must write it down on a bit o' paper, an' show it written to passon and registrator. A cheeld 'ouldn't have no luck in life at all if 'ee was to speak the name out avore the Optimize." " That's true," Mrs. Watts assented. " I've heard as much from my grambnother : an' who'd ought to 'a known about luck if Ole vor her mother was a gipmy-'ooman." " Lard bless the 'ooman, wot's the odds o' all that ?" .Awlfura exclaimed with some contempt. (Ho was a sad free-thinker). " What differ 'II that make to her l Hoed be all-so-well, I aim, if 'ee speaked her name out. She 'ouldn't take no harm : I'll be bound alio 'auldn't. I'll bet 'eo a vi-pun-note upon it." Which was generous of Awlfurd, as the femsimple of his home and the goodwill of his broom blvdtkess would hardly have tunounlod to ten times that sum between them. Lucy crumbed him with 0. glanee. Both were brought_ up as children on the self-same Dorset moors : both roamed Use srune woods, barefooted and bareheaded : both lenrned the 8/11110 lsiiu,iuuiusmms of book-lore and school- knowledge. Their lives have been crest alike sonong the same rough uplend folk, in the cons- any of poachers,' gipsies, horse-misers, and tin- kers. She is in body and mina a splendid example of the practical, flOti,ve, unimpassioned WOllll4ll, the true busy-body. The neigh bourn describe tier as"us rare hand at us bargain." That !nay be true : but Meriel line more nut in one flash of her dark ayee then Lucy has got in her inmost nature. For Meriet's feelings are sleep and strong, while Lucy's are shallow sind lie very much on the bustling surface. ln person, this typical house- wife is of medium height, Bound of wind and limb, and well-built, save that she stoops not a little, and that her back is rounded. Such round- ed backs often accompany the hussy-body tem- perament. Meriel's head is well poised on the stately neck ; Luey's advances in front of the shoulders its a drooping, posture. And these att,i7 fades are charaiderietie : brooders and' dreamers, like Dante or Shelley, hold the bead quite up- right ; practical men cud women of the quick and active temperament, bent .direct on passing aims, let their heads outrun them, so to speak, in their eagerneems to get there. In earlier cen- turies, him wife would have earned the brinks and the ducking-stool : our milder age permits only au occasional assault 011 her busband's part, when tire tang of Luey's tongue lase grown quite unendurable. The neighbours respect her, but mintit that she can " give it hot to Euery " when eireumstances demand. " I'll do vor 'ee !" she shy ieks at hies. Nothing on Greydown in the way of a social event would be quite complete, however, without Lucy Lockett's assistance as disinterested gym- : iiiser. When she was a mere child, indeed, stood, an unpaid mourner, at every grave- side : ‘hoLuey loves they funerals," /her mother murmured to me complacently. " She's st regis- ter puss for a corpse." he was aware that ". women.volk will have their way, an't here's no gainsaying 'eat "—especially Hot if one of them is Lucy Lockett. Sitting down at the kitchen table, with bead bent on one side,' and tongue protruding between teeth that bit it, be closely watched his fingers as they scrawled the two words. "Mary .Tana." nn the ensen managing alt her own ultstrs ildmirshly, she has plenty of time left for setting straight the affairs of others. She is the best possible charwoman ; e cleans her OWII house and gets her husband's breakfast before she le.tvem home at six in the morning, and then (loess good day's work as if she canto quite fresh to it. As 1 passed, Lucy was engaged in seriabbing a threshold stone, off which, as the phrase goes, " you might eat " already.
"Well, Mrs. Lockett," I said, just to draw bee out. " How's Lizzie Somers' baby ?"

Lucy paused in her scrubbing—no matter how busy she might be, she mid always time for a friendly colloquy. " Well, there, sir," she said, deprecatingly, what could you expect front Lizzie ? She won't bring it up well : she doan't understand how to bring up childer. I be a mother myself, and I know how to do it ... Marine Ann "—this to her own eldest, whose soared white face just peeped round the corner— you goo in this minute or I'll skin 'ee 'Tis a poor hubby, Lizzie's. Not that I'd wish to zay anything agin a babe unbaptised, sir, as is always dangerous, through it's not bein' corned yet : vor even when it's my own. I do al- ways veel creepy about a babe unchrimsomed. It do give one a .turn to think there's a soul to whoant as bain't no better nor a baptiseless hea- then." _
"No doubt it ia much exposed meanwhile," I quggested, " to the wiles and assaults of the Evil One." _ _ _

"That's true, sir, that's true : and though the habby's regintrated, it ain't yet baptised. An' unbaptised babbies—" she glanced over her shoul- der askance, and spoke with hated breath— Merle! Stanley do tell me they'm sought after by the pixies. Not that I hold with all Meriel's old.vashioned ways, no more nor I'd hold with Awlfurd Zuminer's new-vangled ones. I. hadn't one as believes in they pixies myself : I've heard too inuch of 'em : still, weld time yolks did use to zay—" Here Lacy's voice dropped till it Was wholly inaudible. "When will it be baptised?" I asked, smiling. . . _ _ .

- "Au, that's it, sir, when ? Ibe always one vor getting awver they things all so soon as pos- sible. Till is bobby's baptised and its mother dawdled and seined, there ain't no knowing what dangers they be exposed to. Wy, if it weren't vor me, I can't zay the misvortunee that mightn't a' happened on thik here hilltop. When my last gun was chrissomed, Zion Roger's bwoy Wlla chrissomed along o' her, in the self-zame water; and I was. afeard passon, beein' a young man and ignorant, through comin' fresh from Oxford, an' him a curate at that, might chrielsoin Zanies bwoy aver° he chrissomed my gad vor me_ But /was there, zure enough. all' you may take ,your word vor it, sir, / didn't allow no ignorant young man to take no such errors." " I have no doubt," I said, " you could afford the University of Oxford many valuable hints upon the practice of christening." " Thank you kindly, sir, for zaying it ; an' who shouldn't, if not me, 88 has held the Will at the vont, bein' a seventh eon's seventh daugh- ter, at every chrissornin' since I growed up here- ot Greydown ?" " But what dreadful thing would have linp. period," I asked, " if parson had christened Sam Roger's boy first ?" " Wot ? doan't 'co know that, sir ? well, you do surprise me. I thought everybody knowed that. If a bwoy Is baptised "avore is gun, he leaves his beard in the vont ; and the girl, she ketches it. Which is why you zee zo many young men nowadays wi'out no beard to speak of, and zo many weld women with beards that doan't be- long to em." " Isn't that proper papistry ?" I asked Once more, in her own tongue, just to see how tshes would answer.

" Lard bless 'ee no, sir, and more nor bap- tisin' of 'em. That ain't no papistry ! Water in the vont is consecrated water, and washes the beard off. Wy, 'twas my grendvather as twohl sue that, an' grandvather was a Wesleeyan, and 'ouldn't 'a stood no papistry.—But you'll have to excuse me sir : you my Enery cumin' whosun sn' I've got a rod in pickle this evenin' cgin Essery.—lfere, Essery, you proper twoad, wot beest 'ee skulking away behinti the house like that vor Jest you come whoam an' vaee the music like a mass. If 'ee doaset, I'll vollow 'ee down to Cat an' Viddle, an' have it all out with 'ee avore landlord and coompany !"

I pitied poor Etter)+, and went my way, sym- pathising. Next morning, blri4. Lockett intd had cut over her left eye : but the neigkbourm shook their heads and murmured with a sigh, " It's main rough on Euery."

div.head: APOLLO PRIZE CHOIR.
div.p: APOLLO PRIZE CHOIR.
Successful Annual Concert.

The Warrington Apollo Prize Male Choir is one of those useful organizations ;which do much to foster a love of good music in the town and the complete success, of the annual concert, held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening, was gratifying to the members of the choir suet all who are interested in its progress. With such ant exceptionally attractive programme as the promoters had arranged, it was not surprising that the hail was filled in every part. The audience, too,was appreciative to a marked degree and encores were the order of the evening. The choir, which since its formation in October 1900, has carried off over £lOO in' prizes, fully maintained its reputation and. is deserving of the highest praise for a series of interpretations which disclosed careful train- ing. The voices were well balanced, the singing was , expressive,and the attention to detail produced exceed-. ingly pleasing effects. Most of the items were test pieces at the Blackpool Musical Festival, and it speaks I volumes for the vocalists that they were able to present them in a way which not only interested the audience throughout, but called forth the warmest approval. The most difficult composition attempted was " The old' soldier's dream " (Cornelius) which abounds In intrica- cies, but the choir acquitted themselves creditably in that particular work as in alllthe others. That favourite' i chorus •' Crossing the plains " (Price) brought ! out the full resources of the choir' and the j wailing music of " From the Sea " (McDowell)- was adequately interpreted. Two gems of harmony were the part songs " Evening's Twilight " end j "Absence ' (Hatton) and the pathos of "The soldier's farewell " (Krasue) impressed the audience. A word of praise must be accorded Mr. Harry Berrey who, as conductor, was largely responsible for the- ' success of the choir's efforts. The solo vocalists—Miss ' Annie Goodwin (soprano), Mr. Harry Berroy (tenor) and Mr. Arthur Weber (bass)--were heard at their best. Miss Goodwin's sweet and flexible voice found full. scope in " At my window " (Henry Parker) and " I was dreaming " (Juncker) and she had the honour a a , recall for each. Mr. Harry 13errey delighted the assembly with a feeling rendering of the old scotch air "Bonnie banks o' Loch Lomond" and responded to an encore with Mary of Argyle." Later in the evening he gave" The Veteran's Song " (Adams) with fine spirit, and the singing by the full choir of toe recurring strains" Long live the King" heightened the' effect. Mr. Arthur Weber is deservedly a favourite with Warrington audiences, and he had a very cordial greet- ing. He is possessed of a powerful voice, and was par- ticularly good on the lower register. He did full justice to the songs In sheltered vale " (D'Alquent and" The Raft" (Fiesta i), the contrasted tones of des- pair and joy in the latter, appealing strongly to his' hearers. As an encore item Mr. Weber gave the stirring "Old Soldier's Song." The promoters had been fortu- nate in securing the services of Mr. Paley. the champion cornet soloist of the world, whose selections were certainly a treat in themselves. He has a complete mastery of the instrument and his artistic renderings of familiarairs with variations were received with remarkable enthusiasm. The humorous element was entrusted to Mr. Wilson 131ackledge and tho choice. was a most happy one. By songs and sketches he kePt the audience in continual merriment, his mimicry beiug? particularly laughable. The duties of accompanists, were well discharged by Mr. E. Wilkes, A.L.C.M. and: Master W. Pearse.

Wigan—Mason, back; Leytham, Jenkins, Carey, and Lowe, threepuarter backs; Anderson and Thomas, half backs ; Watkins, Barton. Little, Tyrer, Ramsdale, Whittaker, Moores, and Brookes; forwards. Warrington—Hallam, back • Kenyon, Isherwood, Jordan, and Harris, three-quarter backs_; Brooks and J. Davies, half-backs; Preston, Thomas, Boardman, Swift Belton, Jolly, Harmer' and Cook, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Smith, Widnes. Touch judges, Messrs. A. Cross, Preston, and W. Mainwaring, Salford. Warrington lost the toss and Preston started against a good breeze. Play immediately settled in the home quarter where Warrington set up a vigorous attack. The forwards quite overplayed the home eight and Brooks and Davies were very active in getting the threequarters on the move. Davies got away cleverly on the touch side and passed to Harris who beat Latham but was short of speed or he would have reached the line. Ari it was he kicked and Mason secured smartly near the posts. Vigorous play here followed and after Davies had been collared on the line, the ball was sent across through the bands of Jordan and Isherwood to Kenyou. The latter was tackled but by a great effort he struggled over the line at the corner with a try. Preston failed at goal. Warrington con- tinued to hold the upper hand and some very smart play was indulged in. Brooks and Davies again got Harris away, and the wing man after a good sprint was somewhat easily captured on the goal line by Mason. Misfortune now befell Warrington. Thomas, Brooks and Kenyon were all injured in turn, and the latter so severely that he had to retire from the game. Wigan rallied after this, and Latham and Jenkins had a glori- ous chance but. Harris spoiled their combination. On the other wing Thomas distinguished himself by beat- ing Lowe and transferring play to the Wigan half. Up to the interval Warrington quite held their own and were leading by a try to nil when the teams crossed over. On resuming the Wigan men made great efforts, and the seven Warrington forwards began to flag somewhat. , Play was quickly taken to the line and though Thomas effectually stopped Lowe, his namesake on the Wigan side cleverly got over from the scrummage and placed Wigan on even terms. Warrington made a line spurt to the other end and both Jordan and Thomas came near scoring. Wigan, however, got the upper hand, and liallam being hampered by his own forwards at half way missed the ball and left Lowe with a clear run in. No goal followed, but the homesters continued to attack, and after J. Thomas had been held on the line. Latham secured near centre and scored a fine try single- handed. The position was a good one, end Mason kicked a goal. Final, Wigan. 1 goal, 3 tries (11 points), Warrington 1 try (3 points.)

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 30,
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 30,
THE...
WHITE ROSE.
By GERALD BISS.
CHAPTER XIV.
THE next morning was bright and frosty, and the wintry sun shone out with unusual vigour.. _ . _ _

It was the kind of• day that begets the desire of exercise in the healthily constituted: and soon after breakfast Bina donned her furs and slipped out of the house for a brisk walk. Unconsciously her steps turned to- wards the Park in her eagerness to get out of the crowded streets. Life seemed to her unusually pleasant, as the blood surged through her, veins; and the cold air exhilarated her as she breathed its freshness. She was thinking 2i nothing in particular, but happy thoughts seemed to chase each other at random through her mind, and through all .ran a subconscious feeling of something new, which lent colour to the whole. All she realised was that she was young and happy, and sufficient for the moment was the sheer joy of living: As an antidote to the cold she was walking fast, and the ground rang hard beneath her feet. By her side , trotted her Irish terrier, Mike, her .faithful companion, whose only grudge against society was that it (lid not receive him at all times with his mistress. To have her alone, and out for a walk reminded him Of the cduntry; in which his whole canirie soul delighted. "Go on, Mike," She cried, as they reached the grass, and off he started, running in gradually diminishing circles and almost falling over himself in the exuberance of his spirits. He returned to her side, pulling and panting with his mouth open, and then started off again on his mad career. She was sc 'intent watching him at play that she did not notice the approach of a man in'a dark tweed -suit, who quickened his, pace as he recognised her.
-"Row early you are out ! " he said, raising his hat,

Bina turnco round with a sudden start. "Lord Ben Nevis ! " she exclaimed, hold- ing out her hand With a smile of welcome. " How you startled me I " , "I'm sorry," he said, laughing, as he took her hand eagerly; "and yct I'm glad. I first noticed your dog careering Wildly round and round, and then -1 recognised. yoU.' "Not too complimentary to me," she said, making a little face. " You had your back to me," replied Ben Nevis, excusing himself, "and I did not expect you out so early." Why not ? " asked Bina. "It's a lovely morning, so I thought I'd take Mike for a run round the park." "Will you take me, too ? " " If you like. I don't suppose Mike will object, though he prefers me to myself." "Wise dog ! " rejoined tho other laughing, "but he'll have to put up with me, now that I have your premission." "I enjoyed myself so much last night," he went on, as they started on their walk. "What did you think of the piece ? " she asked, fencing. " Oh, the piece ? " he said, a little blankly. "Oh, yes, it was very good, of course, but—" "I thought it awfully clever," said Bina decisively: so did Aunt Grizelle." "How charming your aunt is 1 " said her companion in a tone of conviction. "It was so kind of her to ask me down for the week- end." "I hope I shall be able to come," said the girl tantalisingly, Watching his face covertly. "Oh, I thought it was arranged," he began

" Pr.ur Oddingly." " A really good minister." " Poole—Mornington—Duval." " What does the White Rose mean? Such were the exclamations and comment from scores of lips; and anxiety and excite- ment was written on every face. Meanwhile, Bina remained where 13en Nevis had placed her, with Mike by her side, looking up into her face, panting and wagging his tail—the only unconcerned being in the crowd.

A strange idea passed through the girl's mind, an idea so preposterous as to be im- mediately dismissed as absurd. A coinci- dence, she argued, an unfortunate coinci dence, that was all. But the mere suggestion drove all the colour from her face and seemed for an instant to paralyse the action of her heart. Her next thought was a hope that it would occur to no one else—it was too utterly ridiculous.

She herself could not even translate the vague idea into ' a definite form. Then the blood rushed back tenfold into her white face, and she felt hot all over at the absur- dity of the flitting thought. ' " Well ?" she said, through her dry lips, as Ben Nevis returned. -

"I fear it's only too true," he said in a low voice, as he opened the paper, - "Read it," she murmured, again uncon- sciously resting her hand on his arm. "This morning," he read, "at nine o'clock, a terrible discovery was made at Acacia Villa, Wilderness Road, Shepherd's Bush. "As the tenant, Mr. George Elliott, was leaving the house on his way to the City, he discovered the body of a man huddled up amongst the bushes on the right-hand side of the gate. Upon closer examination the man, who was in evening dress', proVed to be dead —and frozen quite stiff. To his horror, Mr. Elliot noticed in his buttonhole the fatal em- blem of a WHITE ROSE!

" The police were immediately sent for: and in a few minutes an inspedfor was on the spot. He was closely followed by the divisional surgeon, who notified that death was due to a stab in the heart and had taken place several hours before. It was impossible, owing to the frozen state of the body, to state exactly how long : but it was probably from six to ten hours.
'The horror of the discovery was intensi- fied by the prompt recognition, of the corpse as that of Lord Oddingly, the Secretary o State for War.
"In every respect the murder was similar to those of Mr. Duval, Lord Poole, and Sir Henry Mornington ; and little doubt exists that It is the fourth of a series.

" The only important point gained, so far as could be ascertained by a cursory exam- ination, was the probability that the murder had been cominitted some distance away and the corpse deported to Shepherd's Bush. A fact which pointed to this waa that the scarf of the deceased peer had been folded into a pad and placed over the wound with a view to absorbing the blood. But the mode and time of transit is at present ob- scure.

"No suspicion attaches to the inhapitante of Acacia Villa, though it is considered quite possible that the murder may have taken place in the immediate neighbourhood. • "Steps are being taken to trace 'Lord Oddingley's movements last night after he left the House of Lords, which was between To and II p.m. "Sir Hugo Verschoyle and a large staff are on the spot. "Fuller details will be given in our later editions." Ben Nevis read to the end in a low voice. "How horrible ! " murmured Bina. " Have—have they any comments? " "Yes, there is a short note," said Ben Nevis. "It runs: The White Rose mur- ders are the most profound sensation of this or any other century: and the whole country is shaken to the very foundations by this suc- cession of horrors. The police confess them- selves completely baffled and, under the circumstances, we are hardly in a position to offer a solution to this problem of bloodshed. Of one thing only we are certain : that behind it there is some very deep and unex- pected reason, which will one day be laid bare. This is no ordinary problem for the detective or common-place series of crimes, but there is some grave cause at work. The only other feasible solution is that they are the work of a criminal lunatic of ,the type of "Jack the Ripper," in London, or Joseph Phillippe, in Paris. The great question is, if the police do not soon unravel the mystery, 'WHO WILL BE THE NEXT ?' " These is nothing more at present," he concluded, "except an obit- uary notice of Lord Oddingly." "How horrible," repeated Bina, tightening her grip on his arm. "will you take me home ? '

! The crowd had assumed alarming propor- tions during the few minutes occupied by the reading: and a murmur of low, but excited conversation rose on- every, side like the buzz of angry bees. "They would lynch the perpetrator if they could find him," said Ben Nevis, slipping the girl's hand tightly into his arm. "Stick close to me while we get out of this." Bina obeyed without a murmur. Little by little Ben Nevis edged his way to the right, gradually leaving the crowd behind: and, despite the horror of the circumstances, he could not help feeling elated, as Bina . . , clung confidingly to his arm, her body pressed close to his by the exigencies of the crowd. It was, however, with a feeling of relief that !he got her safely across the road by St. George's Hospital, where they paused to take ! breath.

" I hope you are not frightened," he whis- pered, bending his head close to hers. "Oh, no," she answered frankly, as she recovered her self-possession, " not with you. You are so cool ana strong." , No compliment is More pleasing to a man: and it was Ben Nevis's turn to flush under his bronzed skin.
" I ask no greater hour or privilege than to protect you,'' he said, in a low voice. At that moiiieilt the persistent hoot-hoot of a motor travelling swiftly interrupted their .conversation.
Beside the. driver 'sat., a mail with white, stern face, who looketrneither to the right nor to the left. '

"Sir Hugo Vcrschoyle!" exclaimed Ben Nevis. , "Poor Sir Hugo," s, cid Bina. " 1 hope to God tke; crowd won't recognise him ! "said her- companion in a voice of sup- pressed excitethent. • " They are in ,an angry mood."
The car was cutting across the coiner into St. 'James's Park, and the crowd divided as if by magic-to give it room. Suddenly someone recognised the occupant with the set face. . -

Verschoyle," he cried out loud. "By God, it's Verschoylc ! " The crowd took up his cry and began to. ' groan and hoot in their excitement. Some- how, of a sudden', the crowd seemed less inclined to let the 'Car through, and by degrees the Chaffeur was forced to slow down and eventually to stop altogether. In a second the ,fnotdr was surrounded by an angry, groaning, hooting mob, which surged nearer and nearer until it looked as though the car 'would be swamped.. ; It only needed a spark to set the whol3 crown aflame. The few police on the spot welt: powerless and were more than outnumbered by a nitib of hooligans,, who had made their way up West to see the excitement. . For an instant the rituation looked serious: and a riot—perhaps worse—hung in the balance.

• Then, with his face whiter than ever, Sir Hugo Verschoyle rose in his seat and faced the angry crowd.. He gazed at them for a full minute with- out flinching : and it felt like a lifetime, • Then, with an : imperative gesture, he raised his hand for silence.

Ile seemed to 'dominate the mob with his personality' and suprine self-possession : and by degrees the .groans and .hoota grew less till silence fell upon them. He stood. there, a single figure in the midst of a hostile ;mob, glancing round with the calmness born;of a great anger. "Give me a hearing." he demanded, in a

Iloud, clear Voice, alter a second or tense silence, " give me a hearing : that is all I ask. Do you call yourselves Englishmen and con- demn a man unheard? You arc angry with rne because I, as head and chief representa- tive of the police, have not yet brought tc justice the murderers of Mr. Duval, Lord Poole. Sir Henry Mornington. and Lord Odeiingly. I have just left the body of the last named, an old and valued personal friend of my own: and I can assiire you that the failure is to me, personally, far more bitter than it can be to any of You. It has not yet been given to us to read thi riddle of these awful crimes ; but, as I stand here, I assure that the time will come, and that it will n. t be very far off. These murders have been carried out with consummate organisation and skill, and there are unknown forces at work which have yet to be fathomed. To do so is* my first duty in this world, and I assure •von, before God, as an Engliskman, I will not spare life or limb to brill/ these murderers to justice, even though it should cost me my own life." His voice rose towards the end of his speech till it vibrated with passion : and it was obvious to all how deeply he was moved. By the strength of his personality he had dominated the crowd, and by the depth of 'his feeling he carried it with him. As he concluded, a tense silence again reigned for a second. Then Lord Ben Nevis sprang forward, realising that the mob only wanted a leader. "Bravo, bravo," he cried, waving his hat in his hand. f' Three cheers for Sir Hugo Verschoyle and success to his efforts." - The crowd, won over by the unexpected speech and sudden suggestion, broke out On all sides into a spontaneous cheer,. led by Ben Nevis on the outskirts; and an anxious nioment was instantly turned into a triumph. Once more docile, the people ,gave way, making room for the car to pass; and it glided forward Swiftly, Sir Hugo Versclioyle —saluting the crowd, which were a moment aefore were eager almost for his blood. Then, as though by magic, it began to disperse as luickly as it had collected. Ben Nevis, meanwhile, had returned to Bina.. who greeted him with glowing cheeks. " You saved the situation," she exclaimed enthusiastically, "by your presence of mind." " Oh, no," he answered, smiling at het • enthusiasm, "it was Verschoyle's splendid pluck and his speech. But come, let me take • you home: it is not really lit for you to be. out." And once more he drew her hand through his arm with an air of protective intimacy.
CHAPTER XV.
Two young men were seated opposite each other at a large writing-table in the library of a castle in Bayarienburg.
• One was reading through a pile of corres• pondence, while the other was taking notes of his comments or dashing off brief answers. At the moment there was a prolonged pause. .

The owner of the correspondence was intent upon a letter which he was reading through a second time as he puffed un- necessarily hard at a large meerschaum pipe. There was a puzzled frown on his face ; and he seemed unable to grasp the full purport of its contents. Then he read the letter for the third time.

,His • secretary, who had busied flimself sorting a pile of papers and scribbling a few notes, looked up as the silence continued. It was not often that the Prince took so long to decide upon the contents of or the reply to a letter.

Seeing that his master was intent on his reading. Otto von Adelstein took a cigarette from a silver box on the table and lit it, luxuriously inhaling a big puff after half-an- hour's abAinence. Then he lolled back in his chair and watched the other's face with an idle interest.

Prince Rudolph of Bavarienburg was a man under • thirty, full of life and vigour. His face was keen and eager, and bore traces of the impetuosity of his disposition. A frown would quickly succeed a smile ; and a sudden outburst of impatience would as suddenly give way 'to a laugh. A man of strong passions and affections, he was given at times to be masterful, even overbearing, whilst at otheis he could with equal readiness be bent to the will of those he loved.

Of these none tuok precedence of Otto, his foster - brother, playmate, companion and secretary. Between the two. an intense love —greater than that of brothers from the fact that they were not brothers—had existed from the days of the cradle: and, despite social differences,. the two were almost inseparable. In private, at Prince Rudolph's special desire, the question of position and birth was entirely igaored between them ; and it was only at State functions, when it was inevitable, that he permitted Otto to treat him with for- mality. They had fought too often as boys to have any false ideas on the subject, and in many things Rudolph was inclined to lean upon Otto as the stronger both in character and physique. The Prince was a handsome man, with brown hair which curled slighly, and a heavy moustache brushed off his lips. His eyes also were brown, but his skin was fair. His nose was straight, with large, sensitive nos- trils: and the only thing about his face which showed any inclination to weakness was his chin. His lips were full and his forehead high, showing a combination of sensuousness and intellectuality : and the whole face was pleasant and appealing, especially to women. Otto von Adelstein was not unlike his master in colouring, except that his eyes were grey and calm. His lips were a trifle thinner and his nostrils less sensitive : but the chief difference in their faces lay in the chin. Otto's chin was square and determined : and his was altogether a more- rugged and manly type of countenance. His face was firm te the extent of obstinacy: but the whole was toned down by a gay. smile and a good- humoured twinkle in the depths of his eyes. His hair and moustache were brushed in a ntyle similar to Rudolph's : and at a cursory glance there • was . a strong resemblance between the two.

Himself quick in decision and impatient of :May in others, Otto began to fidget at the unusual delay, drumming unconsciously: .on the tabh: with his penholder. It was ,a nervous trick, characteristic of his disposition under certain circumstances • At last the Prince broke the silence, relax- ing the frown and bursting into a merry laugh. " Well, I'm hanged ! " he - ,exchimed. "What an • extraordinary letter I What de you make of it, Otto ? " He threw the missive in question carelessly acros3 table.

Otto picked it up without comment and read if through slowly, realising that it was someth;ng out of the common from the attitude of the other. Then he, too, browned thoughtfully and read it a second time, taking an unusually large inhalation from hit cigar- ette, and allowing the smoke to d its DWn exit through his nostrils. Rudolph watched him with an amused smile, poling away at his big pipe. "Otto laid the letter down oa the table. "This Mr. Frazer will be here &Inn!' was his only comment. "He asks for the honour an audience at .noon." " I shan't see him," rejoined the Prince, shortly. " We: must talk it over," said Otto, im- perturbably. " I shan't see him ! " repeated the other; petulantly. " It's abject, crack-brained rot." Otto made no response, but resumCd drrux- ming on the table with his pen abst.acted4.
To be continued,

div.head: SOCIAL GATHERING OF ODDFELLOu/S.
div.p: SOCIAL GATHERING OF ODDFELLOu/S.
Speech by Mr. A. H. Crosfiela

The members of the Prince of Wales Lodge of the Warrington District of Oddfellows (M.U.) held an enjoyable evening at. their headquarters, the Pelican Hotel, on Thursday evening. The social gathering was held in connection with the recent bowling main, oppor- tunity being taken of presenting the prizes won on that occasion. Bro. T. B. Bradshaw, D.G.5f., presided, and there was a good attendance of past and present officers and members of the Lodge. Amongst those present were Bros. A. H. Crosfleld and Captain George Crosfleld the last-named gentleman having redeemed a promise made some time ago, and becono a fully-qualified Oddfellow.
-7.E.Wit, of " The King" was heartily drunk, on the proposition of the Chairman. SPEECH BY. MR. A. H. CROSFIELD.

Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, who was heartily received, said he thanked them very sincerely for having invited him to be present. Although comparisons were entirely out of place it was a particular privilege for him to address the representatives of the strongest lodge in Warrington of the Oddfellows' Society—a society which was the most powerful among the friendly societies in England. (Applause.) The theme was so tempting that one could be excused for dilating at some little length upon that illustration of what the initiative and the individual effort of Englishmen well directed was capable of achieving. k Applause.) He knew of no other nation where they could find institutions comparable to those great friendly societies of England. It was quite true that a few other countries were ahead of us in their provisions for old age when it came on. That was a great issue upon which elections in England had been fought and won and an issue which they would have to consider and discuss in the no distant future. He would like to say that whenever, in times, perhaps, of greater economy, we were able to face that I humane question of providing for old age by means of State aid wisely administered, he hoped that the great friendly societies and the Society of Oddfellows would continue to be as vigorous and progressive as they were that day, and that the provision for a rainy day would still be maintained by members of friendly societies in addition to anything that State aid could provide (Hear, hear and applause.) That gathering rather tempted him to speak at greater length because in spite ;of whatever candid friends in Warrington might say—and people in his position always had a certain number of candid friends—it was always a pleasure in some small way to try and help on every healthy kind of out door recrea- tion. He hoped that the increase in their membership and strength as Oddfellows during the past year would be maintained. (Hear, hear.) He also hoped that that healthy form of recreation—he alluded to bowls, which was par excellence one of the best kinds of recreation open to all toilers tin their towns—would continue to flourish and that they might meet many times to cele- brate the progress of the district and distri- bute the prizes to the successful competitors in their howling competition. (Applause.) He believed that they as Englishmen would strike that happy mean, retaining their fighting power where it was just and necessary, and playing their part like the president of the great republic across the water by striking a blow for peace when ever they had the opportunity and giving a push forward to the forces which really and truly made for greater progress and civilization. (Applause). Captain CROSFIELD in distributing the prizes erepha- ised the value of games for improving the physique of the nation, and of bowls in particular as that was a game in which they all participated. Since he had joined the Lodge he would do his best not only to further their sports but to'further the best interest of the Lodge. Huth),"b the evening songs were given by Bros. J. Willett, V. Attewell and T. Reddish. The humorous side of the entertainment was well sustained by Mr. H. allard and Mr. Ernson. The accompanist was Bro. F. Webster, P.G. Votes of thanks to the artistes and the chairman concluded a most enjoyable evening. The prize v-inners were :-1, J. Middleton, Crosfield I cup and medal; 2, D. Bromley; 3, R. Smith; 4, 0 'Taylor; 5, T. Barnes; 0, S. lIeldon; 7, W. Kerfoot ; W. Woods; 9, J. Peers; 10, C. Clover; 11, B. Hall; 12 F. Finch; 13, J. Wrench; 14, T. Reddish ; 15, John Wrench; 16, F. Clare; 17, T. Wadsworth; 18, H. Heys • 19, H. Cook; 20, A. Wright; and 21, F. Wisedale. The committee who had charge of the arrangements, which were excellent were:—P.D.G.M. Bradshaw (chairman), V.G. H. Maddock (treasurer), P.G.G. P. Freeman (secretary), and Brothers J. Massey, T. Wads- worth, W. King, H. Sykes, C. Mountleld and E. Whitham.

The new Anglo- WITHOUT CONSULTATION Japanese Treaty OF PARLIAMENT. will be generally aocepted,as,indeed it must be. It is an instrument definitely con- ducts& It binds: us for ten years to come. Criticism, however much it might be called for, can now avail nothing. We have entered upon a great, an epoch-making departure in world- policy. We are allied with an Asiatic Power for purposes of mutual defer.ce. We may be called upon to go to war where we have no cause of quarrel except that our co-signatory of the Treaty has been attacked. The defence of India is to become a Japanese interest, and China is to be defended by ourselves and our ally not only against such appropriations as Manchuria by Russia, but also, we presume, against such arrogant seizures as that which was made by Germany on the occasion of the murder of two of her missionaries. So far-reach- ing a Treaty as this makes a radical altera- tion in the structure of Europe. It will have im- measurably greater effect here than in the Far East It is an instrument not only of great potency, but of an importance which it is scarcely possible to exaggerate. That proposals involving such vast responsibilities, ;and of so wide a significance, should have been laid before Parliament before they assumed their present irrevocable form is something that should go without saying. With the Crown, it is true, the Treaty-making power ultimately rests. There is no actual obligation to consult Parliament. Ministers are answer- able to that body for the advice they may give to the KING; but in such matters they are in nowise bound to ask for the consent and approval of Parliament beforehand. Let al. this be granted, and what then ? The con sultation of Parliament as to affairs of such magni- tude is a practice which has grown into our system in such a manner that it may be said to have become a part of the Constitution. Previous to Mr. BAnFona no Prime Minister of late days would have dreamt of concluding such an instru- ment as the Anglo-Japanese Treaty without first taking the sense of the nation on the subject. Mr. Bersourt's statesmanship has been marked throughout by a tendency to flout and to diminish the authority of Parliament. When he was Chief Secretary for Ireland he was accustomed to wait until the House rose for the recess before resorting to sharp measures of coercion. Usually, Parlia- ment was not in session when meetings were broken up, such peaceful orators as Mr. WILFRID BLUNT were arrested and the police were" not to hesitate to shoot." When Parliament did meet the edge of its resentment had worn off, and Mr. BALFOUR learnt the lesson that if a Minister 11 wishes to do what is irrevocable ho should do it I, when Parliament is engaged in shooting the sacred birds. Treaty is nut the only incident which calls for these remarks. There is also the partition of Bengal, an impending event which is creating more excitement and discontent in India than has existed at any time since the Mutiny. The House I, of Commons separated under the clear understand- ing that this was a matter which it should have an opportunity of discussing frilly before the partition was carried into effect. Mr. BRODRICK now says that he only promised to lay papers 'on the table. That was, perhaps, the literal sense of his words; but both the implied and the actual sense was that nothing should be done until the House had expressed its opinion. It was on that understanding that a motion for the adjournment was withdrawn The partition of Bengal is to be carried out as soon as the necessary arrangements can bo made, and when Parliament meets there will be another case in which something has been done that is beyond recall, and in which criticism will be not only belated, but useless. Mr. BALFoures self- approval is so strong that he no doubt calls this great statemanship. Parliament hinders him ; therefore in great affairs of State he will have none Of it, if in any wise its interference is avoidable. This reliance on one's own wisdom is superb as a spectable, no doubt; but it is a danger to the State, aria it is a practical abolition of Parliamen- tary Government. And that is one more strong reason why the men at present in power should go.

Our Irish friends mustered in IRISH strong force at Parr Hall,last (Thurs. Pourrcs, day) evening, and had a most success• ful meeting notwithstanding the very regrettable fact that the guest of the evening, Mr. Joseph Devlin, M.P., was unable to be present. Mr. Devlin is aecretary to the Irish Parliamentary

party and was detained in Dublin at an important meeting of that body. He has,:however, definitely promised to visit Warringtoe,and in all prob- ability he, and Arr. Swift Mac Neill M.P., will address a Parr Hall audience in about a month's time. The speeches on Irish politics which fell from the lips of Mr. O'Donnell M.P., and Mr. J. Nolan M.P., Mr. Farley, and others proved both ' interesting and stimulating to the Irish electors who were present in large numbers. Home Rule was as much to the front as ever, and there was a passionate appeal from Mr. O'Donnell for the privilege and right of self-government by the people of Ireland. The late Lord Salisbury once said that what Ireland required was "twenty years of resolute government." It was pertinently pointed out that the country bad been "resolutely" governed from the Tory standpoint but all the repressive legislation had not succeeded in stamping out the demand for Home Rule. "As long as there is one Irishman true to his country tho demand will continue to be mane" was a phrase which is eloquent of Celtic determination. It was pointed out that the period of Ireland's greatest prosperity was when she governed herself 105 years ago. airing the past century her population had decreased under the mismanagement of English statesmen and now—the irony of it !—her depleted race was used as an argument for reducing Irish repre- sentation in Parliament! Truly the injustices to Ireland were made very real last night, and the meeting should help considerably in strengthening the cause of the " disthressful country."

The annual meeting MESSRS. PEARSON of Messes. Pearson AND KNOWLEJ, LTD. and Knowles, Ltd., always attracts more public interest than is usually attache 1 to such semi-private functions, for the simple reasons that the firm is one of the largest of its kind in the country and that the state of its business usuallyl gives an accurate reflection of the state of trade in the coal :and iron industries. Few firms are managed with such forethought and wisdom, and a scrutiny of the company's balance sheet is a liberal education in sound finance. We notice that the "Joint Stock Companies' Journal for this week has a very timely review of the Iposition the concern holds in the commercial world and makes special and interesting allusion to its financial policy, as follows: "Commencing with a goodwill account of £315,559, the company now attaches no valuation whatever in its balance- sheet to this asset, valuable as it undoubtedly is. The last £lOO,OOO was extinguished twelve months ago by a transfer from the reserve fund,which,how- ever, was left at the eubstantial total of £1.10,000. The balance-sheet lately issued, showing the posi- tion as at June 30, 1905, discloses that of the £llO,OOO now forming the reserve, £72,600 is invested outside the company s undertaking. Moreover, after payment of the dividends recom- mended for 1904-5, there will remain in hand a revenue balance of £8,082 ; so that, between good- will and depreciation, reserve fund, and carry fa-- ward, the company has retained out of its profits a total of £lBO,OOO, or over 35 per cent, on the capital. Actually, it has done more, inasmuch as ; each year's capital expenditure is at once written oft out of revenue. Capital account, in fact, has long been closed. In a word, the balance-sheet, which shows the assets to have exceeded the liabilities by £1,017,267 at June 30 last—the capital, we lopeat, being £Boo,ooo under- states the actual balance in favour of the shareholders by an indeterminable but very large amount. It may be asserted, without a vestige of doubt, therefore, that the par value of shares is much wore than represented by the company's possessions."—The speeches of Mr. Harmood Banner M.P., Mr. W. H. Bleckly and Mr. J. J. Bleckly at the meeting held on Thursday indicate that a general improvement in trade foreshadows increased prosperity for the company. This will be good news in Warrington, for it is generally considered that when" the forge " is in full swing employment is at its best locally. Mr. W. H. Blackly still appears to be enamoured of Mr. Chamberlain's fiscal proposals, but we should imagine the majority of his fellow-shareholders are convinced that the best policy is to " leave well a lone.

There can be no WOMEN AND THE doubt that the FRANCHISE. movement in favour of the enfranchise- ment of women is gaining strength but there is still a necessity for educational work to remove the undoubted prejudice which exists in some quarters. The Women's Social and Politieal Union is much to the fore in creating a healthy public , opinion on the question and one of the most active members—Mrs. Pankhurst—bas addressed the Warrington Trades and Labour Council this week. Although at times she was rather severe on "mere man," Mrs. Pankhurst, who is a gifted speaker, adduced unanswerable arguments to show that women ought, in all justice, to be allowed to exercise the rights of citizenship. There are many questions such as housing reform on which women, from their particular experience, could bring their views to bear with advantage to the country. Manhood suffrage is a pressing reform, but hardly less in importance is the granting of the franchise to women. Mrs. Pankhurst so convinced the Trades Council of the justice of her came that a resolution pointing out that no scheme of redistri- bution which did not extend the vote to women could be acceptable was carried unanimously. The organization which Mrs. Phnkhurst represents is determined to continue the fight, and the members are hopeful that their efforts will 'ere long be crowned wit;i success.
The "yellow peril' THE Tnnuou in South Africa ON TITE RAND. becomes more real

and sinister every day. It appears that the Chinese coolies now at large are to be reckoned by hundreds. There is a continually widening stream of escaped men from the compounds. Tway spread themselves over a country of which they have no knowledge, and among people with none of whose languages they are acquainted. They are destitute and desperate men. Only by means of theft can they assuage their hunger ; and theft is in many cases accompanied by outrage, and in some by assassination. Mr. Lyttleton's idea that the ordinary police arrangements will sua.::e for dealing with such a situation has been given up in a panic. It has been necessary to make some very extraordinary additions alike to the numbers and the powers of the police. The escaped Chinese are being " rounded up" as if they were cattle on a Texan prairie. That is the present idea, at least, of how to deal with them ; but as a matter of fact it does not appear that much "rounding up" has taken place. There are six or seven hun- dred escaped men wandering about, nobody knows where, each of them an object of terror. Over vastly wide spaces of South Africa, Dutch, Eaglish and black men alike are living in a state of nervous apprehension of outrage. There is really a reign of terror in the Transvaal. Such is the state of things produced by the abject subserviency of the Government to an oligarchy of mine-owners in search of cheap labour.

Jangling Neighbours and Suicide. Coroner Brighouse held an inquest at Great Sankey on Wednesday on the body of Alfred Drury, a cask washer at Walker's Brewery, who lived in Grafton- street.—Deceased's clothes and cap were found on the banks of the Sankey and St. Helens Canal and led to the. discovery of the body in the water.—The widow, who stated that her husband was a steady man, said that there was no reason for his drowning himself except that he was upset about the gossip of neigh- ours reflecting on his moral character, The scandal had been carried to such an extent that deceased had been given notice to quit his house.—The Coroner: If neighbours would not gossip so much the world would be much better than it is.— Verdict: "Suicide while temporarily insane-"

Beet, Dl)., will preach the anniver- sary sermons at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday. On Monday he will deliver a lecture on " The reason of the Christian Hope." The Waterworks Contract. Mr. Edward Garside, B.Sc., of Ashton- under-Lyne has been selected as the expert to assist in the investigation of the waterworks contract. He will enter upcn his work almost immediately. Catholic Young Men's Society. The members of this organization have acquired commodious club rooms in the Jubilee Buildings, Horsemarket-street, and the opening is to take place this (Friday) evening. The proceedings will take the form of a social re-union over which Mr. Owen Toole (president of the society) will preside.

,• Memorial to the Late Rev. F. Slater. At Chester Consistory Court on Wednesday, before Chancellor Espin, the Bev. H. B. Firth, vicar, and the wardens of the new parish of St. James, Latchford, -sought permission to fix stained-glass, representing 'Our Lord giving charge to St. Peter, in the third Window from the west end on the north side of the church. The expense will be defrayed by voluntary contributions, and will be a memorial to the late Rev. P. Slater. for twenty 'years vicar of the church. A faculty was granted.

'Warrington and Mr. Carnegie. At the caucus meeting of the Town Council on .Monday Alderman Bennett, as chairman of the Siuseum Committee, reported upon three alternative •,'eheines under which application might be made to Mr. carnegie for assistance towards a public library. It was decided that a detailed report of the schemes should be printed and circulated to the members of 'the Council for consideration before finally deciding upon, the course to be taken. Reeking Rowers Wrecked. An exciting scene was witnessed on the Mersey, at Warrington on Tuesday night. Three men were seen in a flat-bottomed boat behaving in such a reckless 'manner that a workman shouted to them from Fair- elough's flour mill. " Have you got your lifeblets ? on will need them I" The men replied that they had them round their necks, but they had scarcely spoken when the boat overturned and fliey were thrown into 'the river. Two managed to swim to the side. The other man clang to the boat, and was eventually 'rescued.

Personal. Mrs. G. 13111)1-Newcombe of Stockton Heath has just published through Messrs. Beal, Stuttard and Co. of London, a new song entitled " Heigho." Bath words and music are the composition of Mrs. Newcombe, and should add to her reputation in the musical world. The song has been sung with success by Miss Alice Esty, Miss Evangeline Florence and others, An Anthrax Attack. A case of anthrax was notified from Lower Whitley, a village between Warrington and IN orthwich, on Monday evening. The animal, a stirk, was at once cremated, and every precaution taken to isolate the remainder of the stock. The dread disease, which has not appeared in this locality for some time, has occurred in widely-separated parts of Cheshire. Naturally much alarm is felt by Cheshire farmers, who claim that the compensation is inadequate. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE'CLOCK, BRIDGE-STIMET.—Adv,t. Crosfield's Band. This band purposes giving this (Friday) afternoon at 3 o'clock a public perforninnee in Bank Park, per- mission having been kindly given for this purpose by the Parks Committee. The piece played will be "La Cerentola," and the public will have an opportunity of hearing the Band's final rehearsal of this, the test I piece, for Saturday's competition at the Crystal Palace. I Immediately on the conclusion of the performance, the I men will leave for London, accompanied no doubt by the townsmen's best wishes. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS kintcßeT, WA T HRS.—Advt. Sankey Harriers and Athletic dab. The annual general meeting of the above club was held at the Black Horse, on Thursday evening of last week. The hon. secretary's report showed that the last season had been very successful, and that there was a satisfactory balance in hand to commence the present season. The officers elected for the ensuing season were : Coimnittee : Messrs. T. Taylor, A. Howard, A. Warren, W. Waring, and F. Cowap ; auditors, MesSrs. R. Taylor, Jos. Gona..t ; handicappers, Messrs. Jno. Riley and Jan. Potts ; captain Mr. Jos. Riley ; sub-captain, Messrs. Thomaa Devlin and Thomas Minshull ; hon. secretary and• treasurer (re-elected) ; Mr. W. A. Kinsey, 12, Wakefield-street ; assistant, Mr. R. Waring. WASHING AND WRINGING MACHINES try J. S. GAR LAND, 51 to 55 Bridge-street, Warrington.— ADVT. Enforcing the Unemployed Act. The Unemployed Workmen Act has come into opera- tion this week. At the caucus meeting ,of the Town Council on Monday. The Town Clerk reported that under the provisions of the Act it would be necessary for the Corporation to appoint a Distress Committee within five weeks time, to consist of 25 members, and constituted as follows : —l2 representatives of the Town Council ; eight representatives of the Board of Guardians, and five others (to be elected by the Town Council) interested and experienced in the the relief of distress, at least one of these to be a woman. This step is in consequence of the order made by the Local Government Board. PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—AdVt. Funeral of Mrs. Joseph Bissell. The funeral of the late Mrs. J. Bissell, whose death occurred at her residence Gaskell-street, Stockton Heath, on Friday of last week, took place on Monday at the Warrington Cemetery. The officiating Minister being the Rev. C. L. Stcwe, assisted by the Bev. J. Calvert a former minister of the Circuit..' The chief mourners were : Mr. J. Bissell,Joseph,John and Henry James Bissell (sons), Mr. Joseph Mellor of Nes:4ton (son-in-law). Among others present were Mr. John .Thnes, sen., Mr. George Jones, Mr. John Dunn, Mr. George Horne of Wigan and Mr. Patterson. The following gentlemen officiated as bearers Mr. J. Griffiths, Mr. W. Crampton, Mr. R. Bridge, Mr. John Jones, jun., Mr. C. Cotton, Mr. A. Spruce. Members of the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church, were present at the graveside. Floral emblems were sent by Mrs. JamneS Emery (sister), Stafford ; Mr. Daniel Rigby, Manchester, and from a large number of War- rington friends.

Marriage of Miss Norah Fleming. The marriage took place on Monday morning at St. Vincent's, Altrincham, of Dr. Hickey, Ashfield- road, Altrincham, son of Mr. Patrick Hickey, Sale, and Miss Nora Adelaide Fleming, daughter of the late Mr. John H. Fleming, Fleming, of Warrington. The bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr. William A. Fleming, wore a dress of ivory satin trimmed with Brussels lace, with a tulle veil and wreath of orange blossom. She also wore a gold bracelet, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaid was Miss Clarissa Fleming, sister of the bride. and Mr. John J. Hickey, the bridegroom's brother, acted as best man. As the bridal party entered the church, the organist, Mr. J. Howarth Ryder, played the march from Lohengrin." The officiating priest was the Rev. Father Ryder. Mr. and Mrs. Ilickzy later in the day left for Switzerland. The bride's travelling dress was of navy blue cloth trimmed with white satin. There were many handsome presents.

Free Church Council and Workhouse Services. The following copy of a letter which the ltev. S, Matthews has received from the Workhouse Master (Mr. Awbery) speaks for itself :—" Dear sir,—At a meeting yesterday of the House Committee of the W arrington Board of Guardians 1 was unanimously desired to convey to you and to your members of your Free Chum' Council an expression of the committee's warm appreciation and thanks for the voluntary weekly services organized and conducted for so long a period ndw at this institution by your Council. That the results have fully justified their initiation no one will question, and the Guardians desire most sincerely to give official recognition to their value and work, and their unanimous desire for their successful contin- uance. The expression of thanks would be very in- complete if no reference was made to the musical services of Miss Crampton,whose consistent and never failing attendance merits our warmest recognition also I need hardly add that this opportunity afforc's me pleasure to voice my own personal thanks to that of my committee. You are at liberty to make any use i of this letter you deem advisable n order that the the contents may reach all concerned." Astt for CIIN'NINGHAM'S HIOIIöLASS MINBRAL

The quarterly meeting of the Warrington District Charity Tent No. 11, was held in the tent room,Friais Green School, Cairo-street on Tuesday the Nth inst. The meeting was opened by the Chief aulor Bro. Thomas Moores supported by the whole of the tent officers, a • good attendance of .members being also present. After the ordinary business of the tent had been disposed of, and two new members initiated, the rest of the evening was taken tip with a programme of a social character. The Chief Ruler spoke on the desirability of making the meetings of the tent more interesting by the introduction of addresses on Tem- perance and Friendly Society questions and social ' evenings. Songs were given by brethren J. Boardhurst and J. Voden and recitations by Bro. W. Wilcock, and during the evening a liberal distribution of fruit con- sisting of grapes,apples,pears and bananas took place. ' A vote of thanks was prop2sed to the artistes and also to the committee for making the arrangements, and a very pleasant evening was brought to a close about 10 o'clock. The programme for the neat monthly meeting Tuesday, Octcbr 31st will be an address on the " Municipalisation of the Drink Trade " by Bro. J,,seph T3illam D,S. of Manchester, to be followed by discussion.

Volunteer Inspection Dance. This annual dance took place on Monday evening at the Drill Hall, and proved very enjoyable, about 100 couples being present. Colour-Sergeant Spencer and Sergeants Kirkham and Woolstencroft acting as M.C.'s. The music for dancing, which commenced at nine and was continued until two, was supplied by the band of the regiment, Mr. J. T. Richardson conducting. The secretary to the dance committee was Quarter- Sergeant Bennion, who was ably assisted by Colour- Sergeant Clifre (president), and the Sergeants' Mess Committee. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—IINDEB. Railway Mystery. The shockingly mutilated body of an unknown man was found on the London and North-Wesiern Railway near Froghall Bridge on Wednesday morning. It Was convoyed to the mortuary, and later in the day Mr. S. Brighouse held the inquest at the Police Statton.—A shunter named Henry Savage, of Blue coat-street, said he stiw the deceased on Froghall Bridge about five o'clock in the morning, when he bade him good morning. Witness next saw him shortly before six, when his attention was called to the body of the deceased, which was lying face downwards on the traffic siding. The head was over one rail and the legs over the other. The bead was almost severed, and the legs were badly injured. The position of the deceased suggested that he had laid down on the line. Wm. Bate brakesman, 31, Frogball-lane, „gave similar evidence. He also was of optnion that there must have been some act on deceased's part to get in such position.—A description of the deceased given by Police-Constable Dennett was as follows :—About 35 years of age, sft. Gin. or sft. 7in. in height, of rather stout build, sallow complexion, wearing navy blue serge suit, a cap similar to those worn by seafaring men, inside which was the name Atkinson, Salford. He was wearing an Army shirt, but there was nothing on the underclothing to lead to identification. A torn envelope was found in one of the pockets, which when pieced together, showed the name 'Alec Shad. Deceased had the appearance of a foreigner.—Dr. Smith wrote describing deceased's injuries, and stated that death would he instantansons.—The jury returned an open verdict.
