At the Town Hall on Thursday -Mr,:F. H. Tullock, M.lnst.C.E.,conducted an inquiry on behalf of the Local Government Board into the Corporation's application for sanction to the borrowing of £1,200 for the con- struction of bacteria beds at. Longford depiit and ;0,000 for electric lighting purposes.—Mr. A. T. , Holloway (deputy town clerk) made the applications ,on behalf of the Corporation and pointed out that it was intended to construct five bacteria beds at Long- ford one having already been used experimentally with very satisfactory results.—Mr. F. G. Haddock, borough analyst gave evidence and was questioned at some length by Mr. S. Gough.—Mr. Wilson manager at Longford, in reply to Mr. Gough. said there was no stench arising from the new treatment. Alderman Evans said the experimental plant was put down without cost to the Corporation. It had proved very successful, and the Corporation had acquired the bed at cost price. It had since proved so successful that the Corporation desired to lay down the additional beds in respect of which ths application was made. Mr. Rollaway explained that with regard to the application for :‘.:,3,050 for electric lilghting purposes, the estimate was made up as follows: —Over-spent, £I2O ; cable and ducte, Kuntsford- road, £1.,050 ; distributors and ducts, Wilders-1 pool-road, £5BO ; meters and services, z£soo.—Mr. Holloway said the £509 for meters and services would be sufficient for eighteen months.—The inspector suggested that in order to avoid so many applications to the Board the amount of money required for three years should in future bo applied for.—Mr. Holloway said he would bring the Suggestion before the Council. —The inquiry .was closed.

div.head: IRISH DEMONSTRATION.

BIG MEETING IN THE PARR HALL.
Mr. O'Donnell,M.P. and Mr. J. Nolan,M.P.
en Home Rule.
STIRRING ADDRESSES.

• There was a large assembly at the Parr Hall on Thursday evening when a dernonstration'promoted by the Warrington branch of the United Irish League of Great Britain was hvld. Several stirring speeches were delivered and the proeeedings were most enthusiastic. The principal, speakers were Mr. Thomas O'Donnell, M.P., Mr. J. Nolan,M.P.,Councillor Austin Harford, Llverpool, and Mr. F. J. Farley (Executive Council), Manchester. Councillor Maginn presided and those present on the platform included the Revs. Fathers Magrath, and D'Arcy, 7, Revs. H. Donnie°, and C. Harvey Cook, Messrs. Callighan (Earlesown), Lougbrey (organizing secretary of the United Irish League), Sexton (president of the Warrington Branch of the League), Felix Maginn, M. Cunningham, T. Hughes, P. Sexton, E. div.head: CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH.

The'CiralumaN said it was with much regret that he had to announce their disappointment at the absence of Mr. Joseph Devlin, M.P., who WWI advertised to address the meeting. He had telegraped : " Sincerely regret am unable to cross for meeting. Wish every success to yourself and fellow-Irishmen in Warrington. Hope to visit your town in the near future." (Applause.) Another telegram had been received from Councillor McCormick, of St. Helens, while a large number of letters had come from councillors, ministers.and others. The Irishmen who had organized that meeting, said Councillor Maginn, had not asked the audience to meet them to discuss English politics, nor was it their inten- tion to say anything for or against the policy of either of the great political parties only so far as their actions affected the interest and welfare of Ireland. Most of those present had all their possessions invested in England and would in all probability spend the remainder of their days in this country, Therefore they held that they were entitled to be heard as Britishers for they had as great a stake in the country as any citizen of this great empire. They knew the ambitions and the necessities of that country far better than any English- , man,Scotchnian or Welshman, be ho member of merit or workingman. For generations past it bad been the ambition of Irishmen in this country, in the colonies and all parts of the world that before they died they might see Ireland prosperous. Unfortunately it was far from 'being prosperous to-day. It was said when 1161110 Rule was brought forward many years ago that it was only a flash in the pan, that it would de out in the course of time He thought the large audience that night proved that Home Rule was not dead and never would be dead— (applause)—so long as an Irishman who was living was honest to his country. A great English Statesman said some years ago that instead of making Ireland pros- perous find happy with Home Rule he would give it 20 years of resolute government. A good number of those twenty years had gone and what was the result of this resolute Government? 'lt had reduced the popula- tion of Ireland by over a quarter of a ; it had sent more than half a million off the land: it had over- crowded the towns even in Ireland, and had sent large numbers to England to swell the large army of unem- ployed. No Government would MAKE IRELAND HAPPY that had not the will of the people behind it. Irishmen were asking for nothing but Justice end fair play in demanding the liberty to manage their own internal affairs according to the ideas of Irishmen. What did the people who were driven from Ireland become ?—if not the enemies at least not the friends of England. Ireland offered a great field of labour both for her own people and the surplus population of England. He hoped the d 4 was not far distant when both England and Ireland would have land nationalization—(applause) —when the land would be worked for the bandit of all and not for the benefit of a favoured few. (Applause). _

div.head: RESOLUTION.
div.p: THE RESOLUTION.

Mr. J. SEXTON moved: "That this meeting under the auspices of the Warrington branch of the United Irish League of Great Britain reiterates its confidence in the Irish National party in the House of Commons and in their leader Mr. John Itedmond, and pledges itself to continue to support them in every legitimate way in their struggle for the benefit, welfare and prosperity of Ireland ; and that this meeting condemns the attempt recently made by the Government to reduce the Irish representation in the Imperial Parliament." (Applause.) Mr. C. RODDY seconded. They should he said,remember that a great amount of surplus labour was dumped into this country in consequence of the poverty in Ireland. He hoped that Irishmen would use their influence with the Englishmen who worked with them and induce them to discuss the question fairly. Let, them look at the representatives of Ire's, td in the House of Commons and see if they were the enemies of the workingmen in England. When; the Irish members had determined to oppose the progress of certain work in the House of Commons they were told thtt if they continued to pur- sue that course with regard to the Unemployed Bill the WORKING :II EN WOCLO suriftt. _
Mr. Redmoniii;;;eupon ordered his colleagues not to

say a word until the Bill had been passed for the amelioration of distress in the coming winter. In various other • great matters the Irish representatives had alwaysshown themselves to be on the side of the workingmen. Mr. Roddy concluded by urging his hearers to be true to their nation and they would surely succeed i n the end. (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously. MR. O'DONNELL'S SPEECH.

Mr. T. O'Dos•NELT„ M.P., who had acordial reception, , said that if Englishmen wanted an object lesson on I what emigration had done for Ireland, and the number of people who had been driven from that country, they had only to come to that magnificent meeting. But if the Irishmen had been driven from their country and compelled to seek their fortune in England, he was proud to find that they were able to hold their own, to conduct themselves at least as well as the Englishman, and to meet him in trade and commerce as better respected men than they were regarded as being while , they stayed in Ireland. He asked himself at times the question: Why was it that the Englishman and especially the English workingman had that eternal hatred, or to use not quite so strong a word apathy towards the condition of the Irish people who lived under his sway? He would endeavour to show why it was that, instead of having hatred towards the Irishman they ought really to have the greatest love and respect for" Pat." (Applause). Let the English- man carry his mind back for cue hundred years or more and he would see that the men who ennobled the British House of Commons. the greatest orators and statesmen, the noblest and most far-seeing men who shone asbright lights in the arena of British talent, included such men as Burke, Sheridan, and other great Irishmen. Were those men the enemies of liberty in England or the world over? Werethey enemies of the workingmen? No. Whenever their voices were lifted, it was to champion the cause of freedom, liberty and justice. (Applause). England had had a few wars. He did not wish to say that Englishmen were not good fighters—he had his doubts about it. (Laughter.) He was, however, sorry to say that in those wars, and especially in the recent war, Irishmen were among the bravest and most active fighters. From that point of view the Englishman should feel that

_ THE IRISHMAN HAD SAVED HIM on many a bloody field, but even there the English did not always feel that gratitude should be given when Ireland had saved the Union Jack. (Applause.) He (Mr. O'Donnell) did not give credit to the Irishmen for having done the work but he thought it ought to appeal to Englishmen. While England was treating Ireland as she was treating it to-day, he would say to his fellow countrymen that until justice and fiurplay was done they should avoid joining the English army or navy. (Applause.) The great majority of the electors of this country were workingmen, and they ought to be able to send into the British House of Commons a majority of representatives. (Applause.) The English workingtuan had A duty before him, and if he was e tritest and sincere in the cause which he advocated it was his duty to sweep from power the aristocracy, the brewer, and the various other representatives of class interests (Applause.) The landlords of this country stood for monopolies. They held the greatest wealth of the country for a class and withheld it from the mass of the people. The brewers of this country stood, as they stood in almost every country where monopolies were tolerated, for holding that great interest in their hands and they were using it to demoralize the nation and to contaminate and ruin its people. (Applause.) The representatives of class interests in Parliament might say that they got no salaries for doing the noble and .patriotic work of representing the nation and safeguarding its best interests, but they had never 'for- gotten to consider their own interests first. That was human and they could scarcely be blamed for it. (Laughter.) He was glad to realize that there were signs that the British workman was beginning to realize that the only persons who could represent him faithfully and truly in the House of Commons were men of his own class—(applause.)—who had begun below, and who knew the vicissitudes of fortune, and the struggles, torments and trials that the workingman had to undergo. Those and those alone were the men who would be true to his interests and who in the long run would see that the workingman was properly treated. The English workingman might taunt the Irish workingman and peasant with not being as advanced, civilized and intelligent as he was. Did the facts that stared him in the face justify that statement? Ireland was being ruled by Englishmenaceording to the ideas of the aristocracy who misgoverned the Euglish as well as the Irish. (Applause.) The country bad been

laOhitED, AND ENSLAVED I for over a hundred years, and what had the Irish peas- , anti done ? Had-they elected landlords to represent the landlords in Parliament? Had they elected brewers to look after the brewing interest, or railway magnates to look after the interests of their own particular class? No. The Irish peasant had a keener perception than many gave them credit for—(applause)— and he saw long ago that his only chance of I salvation was in electing men from his own class. Twenty-five years ago he did that. To-day the 1 British workingmen were commencing to do it. The speaker referred to the great _part which the late Mr. Parnell played in ronsing the Irish to the sense of the injustice which was being done to them and the result was that the peasants fought determinedly. No doubt Englishmen reading reports which were probably ex- aggerated would come to the conclusion that the Irish were a blood-thirsty, uncivilized nation. The fact was that at that time the nat:on was face to face with a terrible crisis. Their people were on the( verge of starva- tien and the man who would starve before he would fight ft nd die was a coward. (Applause.) The fight began in those days and it was going on now, and he was glad to be able to record that a great deal had been gained in the meantime. England to-day might boast of her laws and the many advantages of a free nation but her land from Land's End to the extreme north of Scotland was as completely in the hands of a monopoly as it was a hundred years ago. (Applause). In Ireland with God's help, they hoped to have in live years hence the whole of the land of their country in the hands of peasants who tilled it. (Applause). Would not that be a revolution whose magnitude Could scarcely be realized until it was carefully thought over ? At the beginning of the period to which he had referred the labourers were

meanest and most cowardly attempt to destroy the representation of the country. There were 103 Irish- men in the House of Commons at the present time but they did not want to be there at all. (Applause.) They did not want to be reduced to 80, they wanted to be reduced to nil. They had a country at home which they saw had suffered from bad government and they wanted to be allowed to give their talents and energies at home to the re-habilation of the people in their own country (Applause.) They had a fertile land waiting for the men to cultivate it ; they had the rivers, in fact they had everything which went to make a nation prosperous and they wanted to be allowed to set to work to make the nation prosperous. (Applause.) They wanted to be sent back to Ireland bag and baggrge for at least 20 years to do their own work and no one else's work. (Applause.) Englishmencould hardly understand the

FEELINGS OF HATRED which must arise in the hearts of Irishmen when they knew that the rain of their country was the result °road government. They came to appeal to the masses of fair thinking Englishmen to remedy the state of things which was disgraceful and ruinous to them. The time would not be long. In a few months only they would have the opportunity of sweeping from power a govern- ment which had been 20 years almost of unbroken reign? Let the working men ask what had the Tory Govern- ment done for England? How much further hal it gone along the path of progress ? Daring the last year it had been in power they saw passed through the British 'louse of Commons a Bill for the relief of the unemployed of England. Did that show that the interest of the working classes bad improved when the last esse nth' measure which the Government passed was a measnre to give poor out-door relief to the unemnloyed ? In tbe minds of all thinking working:nen the Government stood condemned as a government of landlords, Jews, brewers and classes whose only desire was to serve themselves and use Englishmen as tools in the act. (Applause). They would shortly have the opportunity of sweeping away that Government and seeing that the men who represented the people would do Justice to England and to Ireland. (Applause). " I make this last appall said Mr. O'Donnell "though I know that to Irishmen it is unnecessary, when the time comes for you whose inter- ests are in 'lreland though your personal and material interests are here • you whose hearts and eyes are ever tamed to that land, miserable though it may be, have a sacred and a noble duty to perform. You are neither Liberal nor Tory you are Irish, not party politicians but Irish nationalists and the work which you will have to do between the two political parties is to extract the greatest amount or good for your own country and insist that the man who gets your votes shall pledge himself fully and satisfactorily, to give Home Rote and freedom for Ireland. (Loud and continued applause).

SPEECH BY MR. J. NOLAN, af.P. Mr. J. Not, M.P., said the welfare of Irelend depended upon the way in which the people of England exercised their franchise at the next election. He did not say it by way of reproach, but it was a fact that , ever since they got the franchise, the working classes of England had returned to Parliament men who had proved themselves to be enemies to the interests of the workingmen. It was their bounden duty at the next election to see that the masses of England were properly , represented in the House of Commons. From time to time they had returned wealthy men. The result nem inevitable. Those Inda had served the rich and left the toiling masses to struggle on in their misery and their wretchedness. (Applause). He defied any- ' one to stand up and say that he had visited the great centres of industry, and found that the working classes were governed in their own interests. He appealed for justice for Ireland. They were doing their best but the state of that country through the mismanagement of the Government was such as would make even a tiger feel emotion and pity. In Irelaed and in England the system of land tenure was the curse of the courttry. They in Ireland had at least laid the foundation and hoped that in Ireland the system of land tenure would be changed, and that the land would be taken out of the hands of the few and placed in the hands of industry. They wanted to see the working of the land-laws vested in the hands of the Irish People and if they were given the power of self-government they would govern in away which would be a bleseing both to Ireland and to England. (Applaese.) Councillor PAR= said he stood there and demanded freedom for his countrymen as God's right. If ever a country had struggled for rightand freedom and deserved freedom that country was Ireland. They %rel.° an abso- lutely unconquered race even theeeh the contrary was said by Mr. Chamberlain, who had displaced the Kruger Government in the Transvaal for the government of Li Hung Cane, the Chinaman. (Applause.) If English- men expected Ireland to extend to them the hand of fellowship and friendship let there be no parley upon i that question but let Irleand be placed in the position of every other dependency of the British crown. The Irish vote was a power in Warrington and it would be given only to the man who showed himself to be honest and willing to give them justice, and if the man who raised the " Khaiki " cry , at the last election raised an anti-Irish cry. I it was because he heard the Irish vote in England. The nroposal to reduce the representation of Ireland was I the nearest ever made by a Prime Minister. The Prime Minister had been driven by the rider in khaki who had ridden the Belforian horse to the jump. But the Irish leader was there to place the hurdle and down the boree came. (Applause.) He believed that the Liberal party by joining hands With the Labour party would make a Government which ceuld he depended upon to do sonic ' good both to England and to Ireland. He asked them as Englishmen to open their hearts. They had recently I shaken hands with the Yellowruan which the papers had been glorifying why not make an alliance with one who wanted to be a true friend the honest Irishmen— , a friendship which had too long been delayed. (Applause.) Councillor TIARFORD seconded. Irishmen, be said ' were actuated by the strong determination to have Irish liberty. The proposal to reduce the representation of Ireland in the House of Commons, was made in the narneof thehonour of England. The, highest heritaee which a nation could have was its honour, and Englsad should retain its honour and could only retain its honour by giving justice and fair play to Ireland. (Applause.) "

PEARSON & KNOWLES, LTD.
ANNUAL MEETING OF SHARE- HOLDERS.
Brighter Trade Prospects.
MR. W. H. BLECKLY AND THE TARIFF QUESTION.

The thirty-second annual meeting of shareholders of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company Ltd. was held at the offices at Bewsey on Thursday. Mr. J. S. Harroood Banner, M.P. (chairman of directors) presided, and there were also present Messrs. W. H. Bleckly (deputy-chairman), John J. Bleckly, Geo. F. Pearson, Richard Brancker aud W. Peter Itylands (directors), Mr. James Dodds (secretary), Messrs. Herbert Blackly and John Knowles (representing the iron and colliery departments respectively), Messrs. W. Richardson, David G-arnett, J. Paul Rylauds, A. S. Bleckly J. Bleckley, jun., and A. ir. Burgess'

div.head: REPORT.-
div.p: THE REPORT.-

In their report tho Directors stated that the profits for the year ending June 30th, 1905, amounted to £57,183 10s. 10d„ancl the balance brought forward from last year was £6,355 Os. 10d., together £63,511 us. Sd. An interim dividend at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the preference shares and 3 par cent, on the ordinary shares was paid in March last for the half- year ending December 31st, 1901, amounting to 216,275. The direcsors now recommended that for the past half. year a dividend at the rate per annum of 6 par cent. on the preference shares and 5 per cent on the ordinary shares ho declared, making a total distribution for tbe year of £38,659. The directors further recommended that £lO,OOO beadded to the reserve fund, that the sum of £6,810 Os. 4d., which represented the expenditure on capital account for the year. be written off, and that the balance of £B,OBl us. 4d. be carried forward. The general trade of the country in both coal and iron had been throughout the year of an unsatisfactory character; work!ha&been scarce, and on the whole nnremunerative. In compliance with the Articles of Association, Mr. Beck retired from the Board, and was eligible for re-election.—The auditors, Messrs. Blease and Sons, also retired, and were eligible for re-election. THE CHAIRMAN AND THE YEAR'S IVOIIK.

The CHAIRMAN Said he had no doubt that the first point which would have struck the shareholders with satisfaction was that they were able to pay an increased dividend. The two half-yearly dividends together made a dividend of 4 per cent, per annum, absorbing £35,050, whilst in 1904 a dividend was paid at the rate of 3 per cent, per annum, absorbing £32,596. The shareholders would perhaps think they could have been given n bigger dividend, but the directors' first con- sideration had been, as in previous years. the presents- : tion of a strong balance sheet, and they had looked for- ward, as all manufacturers should do, to the fact that they had to consider the scrap heap of old machinery and the replacement of old machinery by new. He thonght the ordinary shareholders would perhaps not consider they bad had very large dividends for their 32 years' work as the average for the whole of that period was only 31 per cent. per annum. The directors had, however, thought first of strengthening the position of the company before paying high dividends to the shareholders. He would like to refer them to a comparison of the ameunt the she reholders received and the amount paid in wages to their workmen. The dividend amounted to £33,610 and he believed their wages averaged £l,OOO per day or £365,000 a year, so that bethought they had a right as shareholders to ask their workers to combine with them in doing their duty for the best ii.terest of the fires and working for what was as much to their joint advantage as to the advantage of the shareholders. (Hear, hear.) They would see from the balance sheet that the amount of goodwill had been entirely extinguished. That was a most satisfactory position. (Hear. hear.) Another item to which he would like to draw their atten- tion was the reserve fund investment account which stood at £72,599 was against £65,933 in 1901. He thought the directors would have their concurrence in the fact that they had regarded the capital account as closed and made all additions to plant and machinery, amounting to £6,810 out of revenne' and that notwithstanding the fact that they bad already depreciated partly their plant and machinery. They had always got. the scrap heap in view , They bad every reason to be satisfied with the profits. from the coal trade. There htel been a diminution in the ' output consequent amen a shortage in demand and there had also been a dirninution‘in price that had been partly met by a reduction in wages of 2,1. par ton granted by Lord James in 1901.Despitethe diminution in output and in price there had not been any reduction in their profits The engineering trade had not been as satisfactory as they might have desired. There was grelt competition : and there bad been considerable dearth of orders during the yell.. Undoubtedly it Would be very desirable if some combination could be formed to keep up the prices in tendering for the work of municipelities and other large institutions, and also if some arrangements could be made whereby the engineer of the contracting party should not be the sole arbitrator to determine the cen- ditions of work and the questions of extras and any other points on which there might be a difference between the manufacturers who snpnlied and those who were receiving the supplies. (Hear, hear.) The condition of the iron trade was slack in the first half of the year but improved hater and the results were considerably better than in 1901. The sales, however, , were less in total of cash received but net in quantity of goods delivered. The railway companies had given notice to discontinue the use of cast iron bosses in the wheels for railway waggona. That had been one of the great parts of the firm's engineering trade so that the change came upon them as a serious blow and necessi- tated that censideration of the scrap heap to ehich he had already referred. They hadmot let the ground slip under them hut had at once made arrangements at a very considerable expense to put up new machinery for the purpose of meeting the demands of the railway companies and the wants of their othercestomers, so as to he able to make wheels with wrought iron bosses of the very highest rituality. He was sure they would agree that it was desirable that the firm should be in the forefront under the hew conditions as they had been in the supply of cast iron wheels and axles up to the present time. He would also like to refer to the reserve fund investment ace.ount upon which they had not hitherto given the shareholders any explanation. Some little time ago they found that in their wire rod trade they had alternative busy and idle periods in consequence of foreign competition coming in at times to oiler goods at low rates and stop the continuous supply which the firm had with their customers. That WAS particularly so in the case of one of the largest. customers with whom they were in close and an opportunity occurred—of which they availed themselves—of purchasing is considerable interest in shares in that company. The result had been most satisfactory, to the contirmoes working of their wire rod mill, as now those intervals of foreign competition did not come in to *item the con- tinuity—and there was no doubt that ccntinuity meant cheapness as well as many other advantages in their work. They had received dividends at the rate of 4 per cent. per annum on that investment and he could assure the meeting that the cantions and careful policy as regarded finance which characterised the firm's own management had also been exercised in the management of the new firm in which they now possessed a large interest in shares. As regarded the future, undoubtedly if they took their experience from the reports in the Press and the speeches of presidents of large associa- tions, they should expect that they were going to have a very good year and be able to present to the share- holders en excellent, report and pay better dividends at the end of the year. There was no doubt that the good harvest of the past year, the peace between Japan and Russia and the generally better- settled state of political matters tended to improve business, and they looked forward to a gleam of sun- shine. Still in thistountry they had no monopoly in trade and no privileges even with the colonies and India on whose behalf they paid such a heavy sum in taxes for naval and military expenditure, so that when good times came they were subject to foreign competi- tion and the good times did not last as long as they used to dn. Let them hope that the prophecies they had seen in the Press would be fulfilled and that, at any rate, they would this year have a better trade in coali and iron which were their sole products and which ought to be of great advantage to them. Before con- cluding, he would like to mention the fact that the Iron and Steel Institute was meeting at present in Shelield and that Mr. Fleury Blackly was one of the vice-presidents as well as treasurer of that institute. It was a great honour to the firm as well as to Slr. Meekly and they hoped that it was an augury of the fact that the pro- hesies of the President as regarded the future of the iron trade would be fulfilled. (Applause.) MR. BL:Cfi.LY AND THE TARIFF QUESTION.

WI. H. BLECK EN seconded. He congratulated the shareholders upon the exceedinglysatisfactory financial position of the company, as shown by the figures sob- milted. During the past year the iron and steel trades had not been in a satisfactory condition, and a large number of their workmen had been only partially employed. At the present moment, he was glad to say. they had a more encouraging prospect before them, and they had reason to hope that they would experience a more or less improved trade in the near future. The so-called Free Traders were now pointing to that condition of things, as proving that the antiquated policy of fifty years ago was I still a \ policy which the Lititish nation ought to follow. Their experience of both good and bad trade there during the past few years proved that Mr. Chamberlain's policy was absolutely necessary if they were to keep their workmen fully emnloyed and pre- vent their own customers from supplying themselves from abroad. He could remember very well when con- I tintental manufacturers were never able to fill their books until the British works w re fully employed. All thathad now changed and English and Scotch works were never as a rule able to fill their books until tte foreigners were working at full swing. That was not

as it should be and he trusted the time would come in the near future when the British manufacturers would be in a position to defend themselves from foreign tariff-nurtured competitors in a manner which our pre- sent short-sighted policy prevented them from doing. The report and balance sheet were unanimously. adopted.

THE DIVIDEND. MR. J. J. BLECKLY AND MUNICIPAL EXTRAVAGANCE. The CHAittmaN moved that a dividend at the rate of 6 per cent per annum on thepreference shares for the half year ended June 3Clth and a dividend at the rate of 5 per cent free of income tax on the ordinary shares be paid on and after the 20th inst. Mr. J. J. BLEOKLEY seconded. Since they met in that room last year they had had to go through very difficult and arduous times and it had taxed all the resources of their establishment and all the capabilities of their managers to produce the results they had attained They might thank very largely the circumstance that they manufactured so many different commodities and that their trade connections extended so widely as to cover almlost the whole of the world, for the fact that they had been able to produce those results, and they were also very much indebted in their works department to the policy of the Board in maintaining the financially strong position that they had always presented and allowing the management liberty to keep modernising their plant with the ells r,ges that were everlastingly coming over the trade. They had had during the year to face lower prices and a rery bare order book throughout. They had had some alvantagee to compensate in the shape of lower wages and cheap material, but it bad been a very heavy fight from the beginning to the end and they, along with the shareholders, were somewhat surprised that they had produced snch good results. With regard to the question of ratesand taxes, it might interest the meeting to knew that the firm actnally ! paid more than the equivalen: to mil per cent, on the capital of the company in rates and taxes, owing to the municipal extravagance, to apply no harsher a term to wnat was going on around them, and ths insatiable rapacity of the tax collector which seemed to grow by what it fed upon. Whether they would ever have any relief he (lid not know. Should Parliament ever be able to spare time from, bullying the publican and quarrelling about the parson, or from their own game of hide and seek, to decide who was to govern the country, it. might bethat questions like that to which he had re- ferred would occupy a little of their leisure and that manufacturers would have something done towards im- proving the very disastrous state of things. There were, indications ahrosid of some improvement in trade. The position 'vas very difficult ' • the improvement was unequally distributed and they had had so many false starts due to speculative influences and things of that kind that they were a little chary of expressing any opinion that things were really better. They cauld however, say that they were equal' to either fortune. If things were bad they were prepared to fight them out and if they were better, the firm was never in se good a position to take advantaae of them. Mr Blackly commended the steps which had been taken to wipe off the whole of the goodwill account, contending that if their example were generally followed there would he much better results in some of their competitor's balance sheets. The amount of borrowed money that. was keeping the trade up and with which they had to compete was becoming portentious audit seemed that the debenture holders were the great sttpport of the iron trade. 't(Laughter.) The resolution was carried. ELECTIONS. On the motion of Mr. W. H. BLECKLV, seconded by Mr. W. P. RI-Lamas, Mr. Edward Beck was re-elected a director. •

On the proposition of Mr- PAUL Itvf.ksos, seconded' by Air. DAVID GARNETT, Messrs. filess.e and Suns were re-appointed "I- a sslarr of MO. VOTES OF THANKS. The CHAIRMAN inured a vote ot titteSS to the secre- tary, managers and other officers of the company at the iron works and collieries for their services during the- year. The results, he said, sooke for themselves, and tbe directors and shareholders had every reason to be satisfied with the work of the officers. Mr. OtiortGE PEtnsog seconded and the !notion was carried.
Mr. JtlEg Dorms briefly responded on be.half of the general &liners and staff, and thanked the chairman for the generous terms in which he had proposed the resolution.

Mr. HEFiIMRT BLECKLY re ended on behalf of the staff in the engineering department. With regard to the opArations in the departannt, he s4id the output had fallen off, that being due to the over-competition, as full employmerr, could only be secured at unre- numerative prices. Their position, however, was now very much improved, but they had still to face the same.. discouraging state of things, for American and German enterprise even in structural iron and steel work was ' being severely felt. Mr. Bleakly referred to the improvemonts which were being naarle in the plant, and poi Ited out that the firm bad had the advantage of an able and exhaustive report from their representa- tives who visited American works. It was encourag- ing to know that the advantages of the alterations and additions now in progress were fully confirmed, and that according to their circumstances and situation they wore doing as well as possihle. Mr. Jomt KNOWLE•3 responded on behalf of the. colliery officials.
A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded tba meet inz.

_ WHO IS MR. OUTHWAITE P• His Australian Friends Explain. Mr. R. L. O&M/ W .11T E's addresses last week MUM such a big impression in the town that his political opponents were driven to the desperate expedient, of' endeavouring to belittle the ram instead of facing Ms arguments. They asked the question : Who is Mr. Oathwaite ? and tried to make 01St that he really was nobody. We have been asked te publish the following extract front the" Birmingham Gazetee and Express ": " Writing from the office of the Birmingham Liberal Association, Coleridge Chambers, Corpora-, Lion-street. Mr. It. L. Oethyraite, the Liberal candi- date for West Birmingham, ask-s us to publish the following letter, which he save ho has rec.eived as aresult (if a paragraph in the "Gazette and Express" in May last : Free Trade Liberal Association, Melbourne, July 11th,190.1 Dear Mr. Oathwa'te,—tienator alathimou has beers good enough to bring under the notice of the coun- cil of this association a paragraph which appeared ' in the Birmingham " Gazette and Express " of May 23th, 1905. In this paragraph it is asserted that you cannot be accented as a representative of the Australian Free Trade party because you oppose Mr. Ca-nberlein's fiscal policy, whereas. many Australian Free Traders are working cordially with the Australian Protectionists for the promo- tion of preferential trading. There is also a further statment : " Also we are informed that he is not in any sense well known in Australia. Matt he appears to represelt is the anti-yellow prejudice of the larrikin class." As all these statements are absolute inventions, they ought to be contradicted, and our council has authorised us to do so. 1. Mr. R. L. Oathwaite is one of the founders , of the Austrllian Free Trade and Liberal Associa- tion. A member of the council of the Victorian Division of this association, and he is a thoroughly representative Australian Free Trader. e. We do not know of any single Free Trader who is working cordially with the Australian Pro- tectionists for the promotion of preferential trad- ing. There are, perhaps, a few Flee Traders who favour a form of preference which differs widely from that advocated by Mr. Charnberleina but even these are not co-operating with the Protectionists. The vast majority of Australian Free Traders want Free Trade, and are oatVosed to any form of prefer- ence. 2. The statement that the Australian Protec- tionists are working for the promotion of pre- ferential trading implies that their whole party is doing so. This is incorrect and misleading. It is as yet doubtful whether even a majority of Protec- tionists are in favour of p,eferential trading. None are in favour of lowering the duties on British goods. Only an insignificant minority has so far ththe any working for itachile a consi clemble section has prononnced against preferential trading. 3. Malt L.Otithwnite is well known. in Nrictori% and not unknown in other Australia's States. For many years he has been known as an enthusiastic advocate of democratic legislation. Mr. Deakin' as Prime Minister, when explaining his reasons for protesting officially against the introduction of the Chinese into the Transvaal, referred thus to Mr Onthwaite as one of the men on whose information he acted ;—" T also received a cablegram from another Australian. Mr. Oathwaite, whom I did know and was well known to,Melbourile before he left for South Aprica." 4. The allegation that only the Australian larrikin class are opposed to Chinese immigration into Australia or their introduction into the Trans- vaal is pure invention. With the exception of a few ultra-Conservatives, the Australian people is united in its opposition to either. This allegation is particularly unfortunate for the Birmingham paper. For Mr. Reid, the leader of the Free Trade party and late Prime Minister, no less than Mr. Deakin, the leader of the Protectionist party and present Fume Minister, are supporters of a Whita Australia,and Mr. Deakin nnd Mr Seddon, the Prein'e of New Zealand have officially protested on bel elf of Australia and New Zealand against the introduc- tion of Chinese into the Transvaal. As Mr. Deakin is the leading Protectionist in Australia, and Mr. Seddon holds the same position in New Zealand your detractor alleges both of them to be larrikins. If it were right, clearly larrikinism and preferen- tialism would be identical in Australasia. We send this letter in order to express the absolute want of truth of the "Birminghttm Gqzette and Express," , and you may therefore mate any use of it which you may see fit. , Wishing you success in the arduous and patriotic fight. : which you have undertaken, We temain yours faithfully, , I F. div.head: LATE MR. WILLIAM GILL. --- Former Warrington Jonrnalist's
div.p: THE LATE MR. WILLIAM GILL. --- Former Warrington Jonrnalist's
Suicide.

Considerable regret was occasioned in Warrington on Satfday when it became known that Mr. William Cif 11, secretary of the Liverpool Licensed Victuallers' Association and a former Warrington journalist, had committed suicide by shooting himself in Smithdown road, Liverpool on Friday night. It appears that the cemetery is much frequented by the public but Dlr. Gill chose a seat in one of the secluded walks, and about dhsk, when there was practically no one about, the report of a firearm startled the stillness. A man in the locality ran to the spot but Mr. Gill's aim had been sure, and he was past human aid. He had placed the end of the revolver behind his ear, and one shot had been suffi- cient.

The late Mr. Gill was very well known in Warring- ton, and was esteemed by a large circle. He joined the staff of" The Examiner " when the paper was acquired by Messrs. Toulmin in 1878. and acted as chief reporter until 1881. He then bought the book- selling business formerly carried on by the late Mr. Truslove in Horsemarket-street, and in 1885 he founded the Observer." He continued the book- selling business along with the publication of the newspaper, ultimately removing to a shop at the top of Cairo-street. When the printing works were trans- ferred to Academy-street, the shop was taken over by Mr. H. W. Naylor. Mr. Gill was editor of The " Observer " up to 1806, and on leaving this town became secretary of the Licensed Victuallers' Associa- tion. He was usually of a cheery disposition, and the news of his tragic end came as a great surprise.

div.head: TIE INQUEST.
div.p: TIE INQUEST.

At the Liverpool City Police-buildings, on Monday the deputy-coroner (Mr. A. G. Inglis) held the inquest. The first witness called was William Frederick Gill, clerk in the employ of the Liverpool Corporation, who said the deceased was his father, with whom he lived at 5, Beechwood-road, Algburth. His father nas fifty years of age, and was secretary of the Liverpool Licensed Victuallers' Association,xvhose offices were in I'earl buildings. St. John's-lane. He was a healthy man, was fairly steady in his habits, and usually of a cheer- ful disposition. At odd times he seemed strange in his manner, and was somewhat morose. Some years ago, before coming to Liverpool, he was engagmd in news- paper work at IVarriogton, and witness's mother put her own capital into it. Unfortunately, all the money was lost, and this worried him a good deal. Ho, however, never spoke to witness abont his business affairs. At times he w is not quite steady, and when this was the case he suffered from had temper and irritability. Same six or eight months ago he was so strange in his manner that witness took certain precautions in regard to deceased's razors, putting them out of his way. His father, however, never threatened anyone. Witness had no reason to anticipate anything wrong last week. On Friday night, he heard of his father's death. Witness identified the note produced as having been written by his father. As a matter of fact, his finances at the office Were not correct.

Charles Gill, another son of the deceased, who was also in the employ of the Licensed Victuallers' Associa- tion, said there had occasionally been some unpleasant- ness between his father and mother over the money that had been lost in Warrington, but beyond this there was no other domestic trouble. The deceased never dis- cussed money matters at home, all the books being kept at the office. There was nothing wrong that he (wit- ness) knew of. Deceased was of a cheerful dis- position but at times he c mplained of a dry, hot feeling in his head. Witness never suspected that he would do any harm to himself. About nine o'clock on Friday morning he left the house to go to business, the family supposing that he was going to the office and afterwards to a funeral. When be (witness) reached the office he found a note awaiting him from his father stating that he was going to Warrington, and that he would bs back about three o'clock that afternoon. He (witness) identified the revolver produced as the one which deceased kept in the office safe with some cartridges. It belonged to a friend of witness's, for whom his father was executor. Witness never SaAV him alive again. He recognised the handwriting on some lettercards as that of his father, and they had evidently been posted by the deceased to the office on Friday. Philip Armstrong, licensed victualler, living at 231, Boundary-street, stated that he was treasurer and also one of the trustees of the Licensed Victuallers' Associa- tion. lie saw deceased officially once a month, and frequently in his private character, and so far as he (witness) knew be was a healthy and steady man. He knew nothing about Mr. Gill's private affairs. Last Wednesday the auditors of the association sent for witness and told him that the deceased had a deficiency in his books. Mr. Gill should have met witness and his colleagues at the bank to transact certain business connected with the end of the financial Tear, but be did not keep the appointment. About eight o'clock on Friday evening he received a letter-card from the deceased, and after reading the contents he immediately went to Aigburth and saw Mre. Gill. but when he arrived at the house be beard that Mr. Gill was dead.
Mr. Inglis : You think that, although the deceased was iinancially7embarrassed, he was a perfectly honest man P—l do.

And that the trouble arose through a little bit of mismanagement of office work ?—That is my opinion. I believe him to have been a thoroughly honest man ; but he was not well acquainted with bookkeeping. Witnes, in reply to the deputy-coroner, stated that the letter he received from the deceased was as follows: —" Dear Phil,—There is a letter for you in the safe. Don't let the coroner or police know of it. I can see no way out of my trouble but tho one I i'am taking. I am heartily sick of life, but did not know I was V. far wrong as I am. Thank you for your many, many kind- nesses. I feel sure you will do what you can to help the wife and family. Charlie is a good lad, and knows nothing of my trouble." Mr. Inglis said that the letter in the safe referred to was of a private nature, and he thought no good pur- pose would he served in making it public. Henry Gough.attenclant at Smithdown-road Cemetery spoke to hearing a revolver shot in the cemetery shortly before six o'clock on Friday night, and to finding the deceased on a seat shot through the head. The revolver was in the man's right hand, which was resting on the seat. He summoned the police, and the body was taken to the Smitbdown-road Workhouse..

—.- The Coroner read a letter which was sent by the deceased to his son Charles, addressed to the -office, Pearl-buildings. After giving instructions for certain office matters to be attended to, the letter proceeded : —" Do anything you can to assist the committee, and I hope God will prosper and strengthen you. You know me and what I have been. I deeply regret the step I have to take, but thero is no better way out of it. Expenditure has been much more than income. . Cremation would be cheapest : but it does not matter, as it is got over quickly. There are a lot of hooks of mine at the office. Do what you can for your mother and your sister, and I dare say you will all be better off now I am gone. I heartily hope so." Another letter read -"I wish to be buried with my little son Frank, and the next grave holds my old friend George Mackey. May the widows be long in coming, and have

increased happiness as the years roll by. I think it will be better all round for me to go. My brain has been like a dry cinder for some time, and I have been afraid of doing an injury to someone. I pray forgiveness from all I have offended or injured, and trust in God's mercy." Dr. Smart deposed that the deceased was taken to the Smithdown-road Workhouse Hospital at six o'clock on Friday evening. He was then quite dead. There was a large wound behind the right ear' which was quite sufficient to account for death. The history of the case showed this to,have been - selfinflicted. . . . .

The Deputy-Coroner, in banding to the jury the letter found in the safe, said the widow declared the statements made therein were not correct. In his (Mr. Inglis's) opinion, there was no doubt the cause of death was suicide. The man was wrong at the office financially and if the jury agreed that this was so the only remain- ing question to be decided was as to his state of mind. That, however, was a question for the jury and not for him.

div.head: VERDICT.
div.p: THE VERDICT.

The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst tem- porarily Insane," and tendered their sympathy with the members of deceased family. The Deputy-Coroner requested Mr. Philip Armstrong to convey to the deceased s relstives thili expression of the jury's sympathy.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOB. MILES.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOB. MILES.

Our readers will regret to hear of the death of an aged and highly respected inhabitant of Warrington in the person of Mr. Job Swales who passed away some- what suddenly last Friday afternoon. Mr. Swales, who was 76 years of age, was born in Yorkshire, but had lived in Warrington for the past 50 years. He formerly carried on the-business of,a brickmaker in Lovely lime, where he had a number of kilns, but for some years he had lived in retirement. He was a very active and use- ful worker on behalf of Primitive Methodism having hold the offices of local preacher, trustee and superin- tendent of the Legh-street Pri:nitive Methodist Chapel. In addition he had served in practically all the offices in the Warrington circuit.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

Evidence of the respect in which the deceased gentle- man was held was afforded by the large attendance at the funeral which took place at the Hill Cliffe graveyard on Monday afternoon. The first part of the service was conducted in Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church, the ministers taking part being the Rev. T. H. Hunt, ex-presieent of the Primitive Methodist Conference,the Rev. J. H. Rollason and the Rev. Jonathan Calvert. One of deceased's favourite hymns" Rock of Ages " was sung and a short- address was delivered by the Rev. I'. 11. Hunt who spoke feelingly on his long associations with the deceased, of the late Mr. Swale's many good qualities, and his willing services to the church. As the mourners left the church Mr. F. Hickman. who presided at the organ, played the Dead March in Saul. The following were the chief mourners :—Messrs. Robert and John Swales (sons), John Podmore, John Broadhurst, Matthew eogo ry, George Titchett, William Covell (sons-in-law), Messrs. Fred and Ben Podanore, the Rev. J. H. Rollason, Messrs Joseph and John Broadhurst,Gordon Titchett, N. M. Covell and N. H. Matthews(grandsons);Jobn Henry, and Smith Knowles (brothers-in-law), Charles, Joseph, Alfred, and John Henry Knowles (nephews.) Others present included Messrs. Isaac Mills, Robert Cook, John Lunt, J. Drury, and I. Johnson. The bearers were Messsrs. J. Shaw, T. Ellwell, E. Mairs. W. Ward. .1. Bailey, H. Malkin, J. Landor, and J. Phillips. The following sent wreaths :—Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Knowles, Mr. and Mrs. John Henry Knowles, Mr. and Mrs. Gregory, Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Ward. Mr. and Mil. Williams and family, Mr. and Mrs. R. Bridge, Mr. and Miss Crampton.
The Examiner, Saturday September 30, 1905.

THEY were having a spelling lesson over at eertain district school the other clay, and the little scholars were all arranged in front of the teacher spelling away for dear life, trying to see how near they could get to the head. The word "chimney" was given out to a little black-eyed girl, who had been spelling words correctly throughout the morning, but she missed this one by inadvertently leaving out the "h." Quick as a wink, the little boy next her pounced on the word and spelt it correctly. "You may go tip one. Johnnie." said the teacher. "I don't want to," whined Johnnie, getting ready to cry. —My mother would whip me if I aid; because I'd get all over soot."

He was 6ned 20s. and costs (£2 Is. in all), his licence, which expires on January 31st next, was suspended until that date, and the bench declared him untt-to hold another motor licence for ono year from January 31st. The offence occured on the same day as the last Petty Sessions, at which defendant was fined for exceeding the speed limit.

In response ,to this stirring appeal, the young lord sent Lit) of his pocket-money, leaving s balance for himself of only a few shillings - By return of post came an acknowledgment of the donation, but the secrelary of the club " begged to inform Lord that he had no* solicited, money from him, and that, if any mistake had occurred, he would willinsly return the £10." Sick at heart, the young lord compared the two letters which he had re- ceived,. and found that ho had been cruelly taken in. Whereas the first letter was written in a schoolboy hand, the second was penned in a manly, business-liko style. The writing papers, too, were quite dissimilar. His school- mates had hoaxed 111111 I He could have got his 1110ney back, of course, but he was too proud to humble himself, and his hard lesson doubt- less did him good. lc] an incautious moment 4 another nobler youth at a southern school lectured a junior on the evils of using slang • when addressing his 4uperiors. It was "your highness" this, and "your highness" the other, always in a mocking, semi cringing style, until the proud boy could bear it no longer, and went off home.

div.head: FORESTERS IN CONFERENCE. ' Meeting of the North-Western Federation at Warrington.
div.p: FORESTERS IN CONFERENCE. ' Meeting of the North-Western Federation at Warrington.

A conference of the North-Western Federation of the ' Ancient Order of Foresters was held at the Town Hall, ! Warrington' on Saturday. There was a large attendance, ! delegates being present from Barrow, Worsley, Audenshaw, Denton, Wilmslow, Prescot, Burnley, Chester, Manchester, Bowden, Altrinchrun. Urmston, Stockport. mud other places Bro. Davies, P.C.R., Earles- town, presided. The MAYOR (Alderman Bolton) extended a hearty ! welcome to the members. Their society existed for , the benefit of the working classes in such a way in times 'of distress that they were taught to rely upon each ' other and especially upon themselves. (Hear, hear.) ;He belonged to the Masonic Order whose" motto ' wa4" Charity." The Forester's motto could be regarded as the same and .by collectine snbscriptions and accumu- ! sums of money to be used. for the benefit of the members in times of distress they were performing one of the greatest charities which it was possible for them to do. (Applause). Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT, M.P., as a member of the i Order, also extended a welcome to the delegates. He urged the desirability of self-help and thrift. Those ! he considered to be the bed-rock at the order. When , sickness or misfortune came the members of the Order had not to look to charity but hail a right to depend upon the Order and the funds which belonged to them. 1 here had recently been passed in the House of Commons, a private bill which was in »large measure favourable to friendly societies. That Act prevented an employer of labour forcing any of his servants to leave one friendly society and join another one existing in the works. Further he believed the Act said theta man belonging toe friendly society existing in connection with a works, who left the works not in consequence of any misconduct,he had power 'to claim to have his share in the Society correctly reckoned and to receive the amount properly due to him on his going away. (Applause.) .. He thought they would agree suoh an Act was absolutely necessary for the welfare of friendly societies. (Hear, hear). ! Alderman TINNION, who also spoke as a member of the I Order, said meetings of t`,rit kind were the best thing for the ratepayers ef Warrington, and he was pleased that the Mayor had seen fit to welcome them at the Town Hall. He hoped the result of that meeting would be satisfactory to the Federation. (Applause.) Bro. Diortrt Horowrov, Grandmaster of the Order of Drnids, welcomed the delegates on behalf of the Friendly Societies of Warrington. Bro. Hulse, P.E1.0 R , of Chester, returned thanks. He trusted the Order would go on and prosper. and that they would continue to benefit the working classes of this country. The Foresters Society was the second largest in the world, and had more than xs,oon.ooo at their disposal. The amount of money paid by Friendly Societies to members was almost incalculable, and amounted to more than .tlOO,OOO every week. He moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor, Mr. Pierpoint and Alder- man Tinnion for their services. Bro. Mum:sit", P.H.C.T., seconded. They did not live for themselves but for each other. They were all striving to do something to reduce the sum total of human misery and he felt sure the mote they were known the better they would be liked. Friendly SoCietieß u'.re triNfrir,, men better citizens by teaching them to understand the re :essity of keeping a close teh upon municipal ano national affairs. (Applause). The vote was heartily accorded. The NIAYort in responding expressed the hope that the order would continue to prosper. It was decided to hold the next meeting of the Federation at Failsworth.

DIE MU TT COURT. Bro. E. E. Farrcw, D.S., :Manchester, presented his report upon the bnsiness of the High Court. From the result of a vote which was taken he said the opinion was growing in the order towards centralization. Ile was directly opposed to such a course as he did not think that in the ldng run it would be in the interests of•the order. Bro. HULS E spoke strongly against the idea of having a central office for the permanent secretary and his staff. A central office would mean a Bottrd of directors and that would prevent working men having the manage- ment of the order and attaining the highest offices. (Applause.)

div.head: WORKERS WITH SORE HANDS. A Hardware Brokers Eczema Cured by Zam-Buk
div.p: WORKERS WITH SORE HANDS. A Hardware Brokers Eczema Cured by Zam-Buk

Eczema often breaks out in the bands of those whose work causes them to handle rough, irritating, or dirty articles. Striking evidence of Zam-Buk's curative power is furnished by the experience of Mr. Henry Kendrick, of 60, 61, 62. and 63, Lower Tower-street, Birmingham who is a well-known general dealer. Mr. Kendrick is constantly handling copper, brass, and iron- ware, and as a result got a breaking out on his hands which spread and troubled him for twelve years. He told his story to a "Sunday Echo" representative as follows :—`• The eruption spread to the wrists, and then came out on my forehead and down my back. They were dry and burning, and I thought the itching sensa- tion would drive me mad. A looal doctor gave °me medicine for eczema, and said I was never to wet the places—not even to wash myself! For two years I suffered martyrdom without relief, and began to get quite run downand weak. After that time the sore would occasionally show a slight improvement, but always in the spring and autumn they would be at their worst. I next went to the Skin Hospital here for about three months, but after con- suming a great quantity of their medicine,and smothering myself with ointment, I had gained bet very little relief. I began to think there could be no cure for it. I was next recommended to give a trial to a local chemist whose ointment was spoken most highly of, and I used a lot of it. It certainly gave me slight relief, but it made no sign of curing me. I was in despair, and I began to find that people did not like my appearance. One day I read how Zarn-Bnk cures eczema and other skin diseases, and I thought I would give it a trial. I purchased a box, and began to rub it into the aff cted parts. I felt great relief from the first applications. The itching and burning began to disappear, and this allowed me to enjoy some refreshing sleep— s luxury that had not been mine for some years, Of course, I continued with the use of Zam-Buk. as I was convinced that I was obtaining more benefit from its use than I had done from all the doctors' medicines and hospitals' and chemists' ointments that I bad been trying for so many years. By the time I had used the contents of the first box I was wonderfully improved in appearance. div.head: SHOULD WOMEN HAVE THE VOTE ?
div.p: SHOULD WOMEN HAVE THE VOTE ?
Mrs. Pankhurst Addresses the Warrington Trades Council.

Mrs. Pankhurst, a prominent member of the Women's Social and Political Union the headquarters of which are at Manchester, attended a special meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday evening and spoke on the question of the enfranchise- ment of women. Mr. Joseph Podmore, jun., presided over a good attendance of delegates. The chairman pointed out that that was the first occa- sion on which the Council had had the pleasure of being addressed by a lady. They were all well acquainted with,Mrs.Pankhurst's work on behalf of labour for many Years past. He had also a distinct recollection of the 'work which her late nusband did for the working classes and all who knew the late Dr. Pankhurst revered his memory. He (the speaker) was strongly in favour of women having the power to vote beqause be believed .that women would be able to bring their views to boar on great social questions to the great advantage of the Working classes. Mrs. Pankhurst, in the course of an interesting And Vigorous address, pointed out that while the industrial position of men had been steadily improving ever since the franchise was extended to workingmen, the condi- tion of working women had been steadily going down. The Union which she represented felt that the question of the enfranchisement of women wanted broadening and deepening, to be changed from a middle-class to a Working-class movement. Mrs. Pankhurst proceeded to trace the history of the franchise agitation in England. Women, she continued, had nothing to thank men for in the way of trying to preserve their liberties for them when the men were first obtaining liberties for themselves. According to Judge- made law, which the Union to which she belonged contended was not the law of England, the word " person" in the Act giving the franchise was held not to include women. Therefore women were not persons in the eye of the law. (Laughter.) Mrs. Pankhurst contended that it was impossible for one sex to legislate justly for another. Take for instAnce the unemployed question. liven Socialist speakers when they talked about the troubles of the unemployed seemed to lose sight of the fact that _there were women who lacked employment as well as Then. They only recognized the dependence of wives 'upon the men and forgot about unmarried women, 'Widows and deserted wives who had to struggle to keep themselves. Women were handicapped in earning their livings and getting their rights through being deprived of the only lever that was of any use—the Paulin- rnentay vote—in getting the evils from which they suffered remedied. When the women got the vote they would also try to help the roan to use it more worthily than they had done in the Past. The experience of home life which women had had and men had not received to the same extent, would be valuable in settling questions of housing, the feed- ing of children, and all kinds of conveniences for the. Welfare of the community which municipalities and Parliament would have to provide sooner or later. The thin that would rouse women most of all was the Possession of the Parliamentary vote and when the ! women were roused the social conditions would be I quickly settled. The advocates of the enfranchisement of women were defeated at the Labour Representation Conference at Liverpool because their position was not Understood and since then the Union had undertaken the work of educating the Trades Councils of the country 'Olt the question. There 'xis no doubt that the Liberal arty, if they got through their programme when they 'Arne into power—as she supposed they would at the next election—intended to pass some kind of measure which would have the effect of giving manhood suffrage but would not enfranchise women. Mrs. Pankhurst incidentally observed that the question of how women veli? worked in the home should he remunerated for their services to the nation would have to be sett led 800 n. In conclusion she remarked that she and others 'lad come out of their homes in order to help in the etruggle of politics. It was because they wanted to make the world sweeter and happier and end the evils which could only be remedied when men and women worked shoulder to shoulder. (Applause.) Several questions were asked at the close and these Were answered by Mrs. Pankhurst. The Chairman proposed the following resolution, which is to be sent to the committee sitting on the question of redistribution of seats :—" That no scheme of redistribution of seats can lead to the effectual repre- aentation of the people unless provision is made for the registration of qualified women as voters." This was seconded by Mr. Plumb and carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. Fargher, seconded by Mr. olley,a vote of thanks was passed to Mrs. Pankhurst ter her address.

div.head: FitEE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FitEE CHURCHES.
AUTUMN WORK.

The summer season has now passed, and Free Churchmen are preparing their programme for the Autumn and Winter work. Free -Ohurch Councils have by no means been idle during what is uSually termed the holiday *season. The Open Air Campaign has this year been unusually successful. In addition to this there have been Summer CJnferenees at Seaside Resorts designed to touch Christian workers gathered frotn various parts. Dr. Horton's Conventions have also been carried on, a very successful one at Cheltenham having just olosed. With the cooler days, however, special summer work will be discontinued and there are many branches of work the Free Church Councils are anxious to undertake. It is anticipated that during the coming season a great deal of attention will be given to Social Work and also to the extension of the Young Free Churchmen's Auxiliary, a new depart- ment which was instituted last year. Thirty of these Auxiliaries have already been formed, and it has been arranged for some five or six leading ministers to tour the country explaining the work and advocating .the formation of these Societies for Young Men.

div.head: UNITED MISSIONS.
div.p: UNITED MISSIONS.

After the summer vacation the special missioners of the National Free Church Council have recommenced their work with every pro- spect of a most successful season. Gipsy Smith, after conducting a thoroughly successful mission at Scunthorpe, has gone on to Tooting. Here the prospects are so good that the local tram sheds have been hired and fitted up for the mission services. Mr. W. R. Lane commenced his autumn campaign with a mission at Bath. The Council secured a local Music Hall with a seating capacity of two thousand, and the place was not only filled, people standing in the aisles, but several hundreds had to be turned away from the doors. On the Saturday evening a procession was formed and paraded through the town, a midnight meeting following. A marvellous gathering of drunken and half- drunken people were drawn in, and the meeting did not break up till 1.30. The Rev. J. Tolefree Parr opened his autumn work with a successful mission at Bishop Auckland.
NEW SOCIAL INSTITUTE.

The Social Campaign of the National Free Church Council has led to some very practical work. At Pwllholi a special Institute has been established as a result cf the Revival, whilst an Institute for social and religious work has been founded at Pateley Bridge by the Nidd Valley Free Church Council. This is a result of the Revival that has visited that beautiful Yorkshire valley. The Churches have co- operated so fully that it was not difficult to arrange for a building to give permanence to this Institutional work. This has only just been opened.

div.head: PUBLIC INSTITUTE WORK.
div.p: PUBLIC INSTITUTE WORK.

Free Church Council work in connection with local institutions is still extending. At Leeds there are two large convalescent homes —the Ida Home and the Arthington Home at Cookridge, some five miles out of the city. They are under the management of the Leeds Infirmary Board, and patients are transferred from one institution to the other as need arises. The Board has given consent, and the Council has just started a weekly service on Tuesdays, under the care of the Bev. G. Winter Wilson, the Free Church chaplain.

div.head: MISSIONARY ENDEAVOUR.
div.p: MISSIONARY ENDEAVOUR.

During the coming season one of the most Important departments of Free Church Coun- cils work will be that of the Missionary Com- mittee. It is announced that an organising agent is about to be appointed for the purpose of developing Missionary Study Circles and generally arousing missionary enthusiasm in the country. The aim of the Missionary Committee will be to foster interest in the work of the various Missionary Societies, but in no case will it develop independent missionary work. It is probable that one of the first things undertaken by the Missionary Committee will be the ap- pointment of missionary experts to visit China. These will be sent for the purpose of an inde- pendent investigation in the interests of all the denominational societies, with the object of ascertaining how far mutual co-operation can be extended and overlapping prevented.

div.head: CHURCH RATE STORY.
div.p: A CHURCH RATE STORY.

Writing in this month's Free churchman on "My Pleasurable Hobbies," Sir Richard Tangye tells how he catne to collect Oliver Cromwell relics. "My father," he says, "was a small farmer in the west of Cornwall, and from con- scientious motives, being a Quaker, he objected to paying Church rates and tithes. He was the only Quaker in the parish, and although he had a hard struggle for the means of sup- porting his large family, he was always kind and helpful to his poorer neighbours. But the rector of the parish, a well-to-do man, must have his pound of flesh,' for the 'law allowed it,' and so, twice a year, our scanty stock was distrained upon; sometimes the cow was taken, and sometimes the store of bacon, laid by for the winter's use. These things were sold by public auction, and on one occasion the bacon was bought by the rector's butler, and re-sold to his master. Soon after the sale the butler came to mot mother with this messaga from his master: 'tell Mrs. Tangy° that the bacon is the best I ever tasted.' Whether the message was really sent or whether it was the outcome of the butler's ' superfluity of naughtiness' I know not, but this Ido know—it gave me an intense hatred of the system responsible for snob an outrage."
DR. HORTON'S DEVOTIONAL MANUAL.

During the trouble with his eyes last year Dr. Horton was led to write his beautiful volume, "The Open Secret." This Manual of Devotion seems to have won for itself a permanent place, and the National Free Church Council now announces that a new cheap edition is to be issued at one shilling net.

div.head: TO CHRISTIAN WORKBRS.
div.p: TO CHRISTIAN WORKBRS.

Gipsy Smith is known the world over as an Evangelist and preacher, but it is not often that he writes for the magazines. The Free Church Chnnicle for this month has been able to secure an article from his pen, addressed to Christian Workers. It is quite in Gipsy Smith's characteristic style, and is a call for inure systematic and devoted work in the direction of the evangelisation of the masses.

div.head: FREE' CHURCH LITERATURE.
div.p: FREE' CHURCH LITERATURE.

The National Free Church Council, realising the importance of the circulation of good Free Church literature, has for some years past been issuing the Free. Churchman as a magazine for localisation. The success of this magazine has boon most gratifying, the circulation baying quadrupled during the last few years. Notwith- standing this, the conductors are seeking to make the next volume even better than before. Considerable time and thought have been given to the, arranging of the programme for 1906, and this, with the specimen number for January, will shortly be issued. The Manager of the Publication Department, National Free Church Council, Memorial Hall, will send sped. mons on application.
