div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 30, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 30, 1905.
(ALL RIGIITS RESERVED.]
JAPANESE GIRLS AND WOMEN,
ERNEST YOUNG (thither of" The Kingdom of the Yellow Robe," 0.)

Most English people have formed their ideas of Japanese girls from pretty postcards and from representations of brightly acted plays such as the " Geisha." They are, in conse- quence, apt to regard the life of the average Japanese woman as resembling that of a butter- fly—gay, careless, and sunny. Never was a more serious error of judgment committed. Jap- anese women as a whole do not. resemble " Mi- mosa• San," any more than Engliskwomen as a • whole resemble the chorus girls of a Christmas pantomime. Let me first tell two little stories by way of removing the erroneous estimate already formed, and then we shall be in a position to glance at the life of the Japanese woman from a new point of view. Story. number one 1805, Japan fought China and won—that's an old story. The commander of the warship Akagi was Saktunoto. When the great naval battle was fought in the Yellow Sea, he led his ship into the thickest of the fight, and there met his death. A messen- ger was immediately despatched to carry the sad tidings to his family. His aged mother met the officer who brought the story, and heard him with dry eyes to the bitter end. Then she looked into his face', pain struggling with pride in every movement of her body and her coun- tenance, and without a tear in her eye, or a quiver in her voice she remarked, " So, it seems by your tidings that my. son has been of some service this time."

There is little of the butterfly about that. And yet the old lady is a fair type of the mothers of Japan. Story number two. It happened in the same war, and the heroine of the tale was just over twenty. She had not long been married, and her husband was a soldier, lie went to China, mid there he laid down his life. When the girl-wife heard of his death, she sent away her servants, set her house in order, wrote farewell letters to her friends, dressed herself in her bridal robes, knelt before the portrait of her husband, stabbed herself to the heart with a dirk, and went to join her lost one in the land -beyond the grave. There is little of sun and careless- ness in that. And yet, the heroine of the story is a fair type of the young wives of Japan.
'MEHL RESPECT FOR AGE.

The truth of the matter is, that owing to centuries of training, the character of which I will presently indicate, the japauese woman has learnt to suffer without hysterics, and to obey without argument. The keynote of her whole existence is obedience, cheerfully and willingly rendered to all those to whom custom has decided that it shall be rendered.

All over the East, perhaps the first thing that strikes the observant European is the respect and reverence with which children treat not only their parents, bat all who are older than themselves. This is particularly noticeable in Japan, and the first lesson the growing girl learns, is to do what she is told by her elder re- latives, without questioning the reasonableness or the justice of the command. The elder sis- ter takes precedence of the younger in all mat- ters, and is always addressed by a title which conveys to the listener the fact that she is the elder sister.

In the next place she is taught that household duties are not to be shirked and handed over to servants. She must learn to cook, to bargain with itinerant vendors, to wash, and to wait like a servant. If her father has guests that he wishes to honour, she must stand behind his seat, hand him -the several dishes, and fill his, glass when it becomes empty. She sees nothing menial in such an occupation. She understanthi and appreciates the glory of cheerful service. She learns to wash clothes, and not to trust them to a laundress. In this operation she al- ways uses cold water, and never handles soap. Instead of ironing out her silks and cottons, she places them on smooth boards and beats them dry and even. She has, of course, no pictures, no dust, and no furniture to polish, lint she goes down on bands and knees, and cleans the outer verandah, she rolls up the folding mattresses in the morning, and puts away the mosquito cur- tains that have shelteied them all during the night. Do not imagine that it is only the lower classes that perform these tasks. Every Japan- ese girl, below the rank of the very highest, can perform mid does performe very duty of do- mestic service when required. She has learned to work.

div.head: YOUNG MARRIED WOMAN.
div.p: THE YOUNG MARRIED WOMAN.

She has not, however, learned to flirt, and she is not " fast," nor does she know or practice the arts by which Western maidens seek to at- tract the youth of their own land. But when she is about sixteen years of age, her father chooses a basband for her, and this choice she accepts without murmur or complaint. It is her destiny. She has always expected to be married in this way, and has never even con- templated the possibility of being an old maid. When she gets married she goes to live not merely with her husband, but with her husband's family, for the newly-wedded son does not dream of setting up a house for himself. In this new home, the young wife is merely a member of the family, and not a mistress. She is at the beck and call of her mother-hi-law, and her tirst duty is not to her husband, but to her busband's parents. (How happy must the girl be who marries a man With no parents !) She is practi- cally a new servant for her mother-in-law.

-- The wife does not -occupy a position of equality with her husband, even when the parents ,do not exist. In this case he is, the housekeeper, the chief servant, the orderer of all feasts mid ceremonies, and little else. She rarely appears in public with her husband, and if she does it is as his attendant, to follow and wait upon him. Even the Empress herself is not exempt from personal service upon the Emperor. When morning dawns, the wife rises first, puts out the light of the little lamp that has burnt all night, makes her toilet, dresses her- self. rouses the servants, helps to get,the break- 'fast, and when all is ready, wakes her lord mid master. When this same lord and master sets out for business, the wife is at the door, ready with sandal, book, umbrella, or any other object her chief may need.

div.head: AN OLD AGE or HONOUR AND REPOSE.
div.p: AN OLD AGE or HONOUR AND REPOSE.

In time the Japanese woman grows old. She loses her beauty at an early age, and at thirty- five heischeeks have lost their colour, her eyes their brightness, and her figure that plumpness and rotundity that help to make the little Jap- anese maiden SO pleasant to look upon. But she never regrets. She never tries to look younger than she is. She even wears her clothes and dresses her hair in such a way as to indicate to those who can read the signs, the exact number of years that have passed over her bead. And why ? Because the time has arrived when that obedience which .has been her chief woman- ly virtue, and which she has paid unceasingly through the days of her youth and her prime, will now be rendered to her by her Own des- cendants. She is now the happy mother-in-law who finds a new servant in the wife Of her son. She may now rest from household labour, and be waited on for the rest of her days. She looks forward to old age as a period of honour and repose. Those who know anything of. the history of Japan, will know that for many years the Em- peror was it mere figurehead without power or influence. All the real authority was in the hands of the Shoguns, and their great nobles the daiinios. These latter were at first serves! by the samurai, the military and learned class, though the samurai became in time flue real masters of thus land, end it, is their descendants who at the present, time are upholding the hon- our of Japan. The wives of ilwse men huve in- fluenced the present gem-rotion in Japan to such in extent fle.r. --,v '''' •,t Janaue-- &omen that tailed to give some short account ot them would be hopelessly incomplete.
TIIE lAMLRAI WOMEN.

They were in earlier times the servants of the wives of the daim ice, for whom they performed the most humble offices, regarding -it as a grand privilege to be commanded by the wives of such powerful men. But they could perform other duties besides those of the lady's maid and the chamber-maid. They could light. When the great noble and his retinue were away from home it was their business to guard his honse from his enemies. On such occasions they wore quilted trousers, a stiff cap and a great spear tover. They could handle the long spears and the short sword, and have been known 0 ilsr,lat

div.head: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
PENKETH.

The harvest thanksgiving services were held at the Wesleyan Church, Penketh on Sunday.. The interior had been beautifully decorated with all kinds of choice fruit, corn, vegetables and flowars,by a number of ladies attending the church. The Rev. John Gunnell con- ducted the morning service. The Rev. Jos. Manning occupied the pulpit at the evening service. Special hymns and anthems were stmg.Mr. G. W. Weaver presided at the organ. LEGH-STREET, PRIMITIVE METHODIST.

The thanksgiving services were held on Sunday. the ehurch being prettily decorated for the occasion with fruit, flowers, &.c. The preacher for the day was the Rev. W. Scott, of Wishavo, Scotland. In the afternoon a crowded congregation listened to a cantata entitled Esther, the beautifullqueen," Miss Alice Bridge taking the prominent part. At the evening service the anthem " The Lord is my shepherd," was ably rendered by the choir' and a duet "Sing to the Lord of harvest," by Miss Bridge (soprano), and Mr. Corrin (tenor) was also given. " On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held in the schoolroom. _

CHRIST CHURCH, PADGATE. The harvest thanksgiving services were continued on Sunday. In the morning the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. .J. H. G. Hollingworth, and the evening by the Rev. J. G. Jones, vicar of Great Sankey. During the day the choir acquitted themselves creditably. The morning anthem was Barnby's "0 Lord, how manifold are Thy works," while in the evening the anthem was Simper's " Let us thank Thee Lord our God," the solos being vere tastefully sung by Mr. Frank Burrell and Master Harold Pass. The offertory, which is to be devoted to the laying out of the new portion of the churchyard, amounted to over £lO. BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHURCH.

The harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sun- day. the preacher in the morning being the Rev. Cecil Parker, and in the evening the Rev. Sidney Pitt. The anthem Sing to the Lord of the harvest," was given at the morning service and in the evening, " Praise the Lord, 0 Jerusalem "was well rendered, the respective soloists being Miss Dunn and Miss C. Hastings. The church had been prettily decorated for the occasion with corn, fruit, flowers, and vegetables by the following : Mesdames Weaver, Harris, J. E. Barlow, Halford, J. Lingard and the Misses M. Weaver, Holt, E. Jonek N. Bailey and others. Mr. Frank Hickman was at the organ.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.
div.p: ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.

-- The services of thanksgiving for the ingathering of the harvest were held at this church on Friday and Sunday and were largely attended. Thanks to the efforts of a large band of workers the church had been lavishly and tastefully decorated and it was the general opinion that the effect could hardly have been improved upon. There was an abundance of corn, fruit and vegetables and while the general scheme was most pleasing, special attention was bestowed upon the altar and chancel, the pulpit and the font. The preacher at evenaong on Iriday was the f Rev. Canon Dickson, Vicar of Christ. Church, Waterloo who based his sermon on the words " A joyful and 'pleasant thing it is to be thankful." There were pro- cessional and recessional hymns, and the choir rendered the anthem "Blessed shalt be thy basket," (Simper). The Magnilicat and Nunc Dimmitis were sung to special settings by the same composer. At the choral celebration of the Holy Communion on Sunday morning, at which there was a large congrega- tion,the Rev. W. Pollock Hill,vicar of Padgate,pre,ached his text being "Giving Him thanks." He drew attention to the cause for thankfulness not only in the fact that the harvest had been plentiful, but in national blessings and improved trade locally. In the afternoon a children's service was held. the Rev. T. W. Barber. of St. Elphin's. delivering an address. At evensong the church was filled, and a powerful sermon was preached by the Rev. W. Brown-Pollock, of S. James the Less, Liverpool. on the words "And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth : and it was so." He spoke of the harvest as being an evidence of the truth of God's Word, of his unfailing justice, and His regard for man. Special music was again rendered. The collections throughout the festival were on behalf of the choir fund.

div.head: RACE BETWEEN FOOTBALLERS.
div.p: RACE BETWEEN FOOTBALLERS.
Fish's Easy Win.

Considerable local interest was taken in the 80 yards sprint race between J. Fish of the Warrington Foot- ball Club and Peter Green of the Wigan vootball Club which took place at Springfield Park, Wigan on Satur- day evening. The stakes were £25 a-side reduced from £5O a-side, and both men had been in active training for amonth, J. Heesom of Warrington being Fish's mentor. There was an enthusiastic crowd of about 1,200 people, a large proportion of whom were from Warrington. Probably the gates would have been much larger but for the fatality to Green's brother on the , morning of the match, this sad event causing many ' people to imagine that the races would not come off. Green was kept ignorant of the fatality till after the race, and of course fulfilled his engagement. The race was fixed for 5.30; but it was half an hour later before the men put in appearance. The local man won the toss for choice of road and side, and elected to have the breeze at his back,and run on the track nearest the spectators. Speculation was very limited, but what little business was done in this line showed Fish to be a pronounced favourite even among the Wigan folk. Mr. Stinton, of Manchester, got the men away to an excellent start, and Fish at once took the lead. He quite out-paced Green, and after taking a look over his shoulder at half-way finished an easy winner by a clear three yards. Time, 8 2-5 secs.

div.head: Town "Beautiful."
div.p: The Town "Beautiful."

Sir,—The Beautiful Warrington Society is a very commendable institution. To look for the Beautiful in aoything is to seek the highest and best, and the objects of the above society are worthy of all support. As time goes on, who knows, but that these preliminary efforts may not be the forerunners of slum abolition and vile hoardings removed. The gaping pieces of land which are now carpeted with old cans may be clothed in green grass. And apart from the mere sight who can comprehend the moral good done to the people. If slums degrade the mind and break the morals of their inhabitants, may not their removal tend to uplift their character and encourage them in divers good ways. The influence of a city or town of real beauty and light is incalculable. May the work of those, who in any way are striving after the ideal, abundantly prosper in the wish of one who is
A lIMIBLE ADNIMER,

What Will the Voter do? Sir,-1 am a Conservative working man, and am as a matter of course (vide Free Critic) "a curiosity." Now with your permission, Mr. Bditor (and I must say in fairness to you, that although your paper is the Liberal organ you have always treated any letters I have written, with impartiality) the" Cariosity "would like to say just a few words in reply to a Free Critic's " letter. Let me in the first place say that although a Conserva- tive workingman lam not considered ignorant, nor do I think I sin a person to be deluded by clap-trap, and to prove that clap-trap doesnot affect me, let me state that I have been to Liberal meetings, both in Warrington and other parts of the country,l have read "Exeter Hall talk" and havd even listened to the" Liberal Parson." I could even give more proof, but I think, dear Editor, the above will be enough for your readers. My friend is great on Chinese labour, like the rest of his friends, but if he does not mind he will flog the poor horse dead before the election comes. Take my advice young man, hold to him a bit, or he will be 'winded before the election comes, and then you'll be out of the running. Yon don't know " Arthur James," he's not beaten yet. He's still in the running although (to carry the sporting term further), the "Daily News" has been 'tipping' against him, he is still in the running and leading. "Free Critic " says, "And are not the workingmen aware that if they remain quiet and take it down' that there is a danger of the same system being introduced in England?" Who's talking clap-trap now? Listen reader dear, what is! (not what might Ke). Whilst the workingman's friends (the Liberals) when shouting and preaching from North to South about the " terrible evil" that was taking place hundreds and hundreds of miles away, these very men, the lovers of the workingmen, were doing all in their power to stop the passing of the Bill which was to keep out the alien from our homes, to keep the Germans from taking our bread. Fellow-workingmen, beware! We have Ge:mans in Warrington, and 1 for one do not think "the Member for Cypruslwi II want'any Chinese in good old NVarrington. To deal with " Free Critic's"" grand final," "Arthur Crosfield, a gallant gentleman and an able politician to

boot." Arthur Crosfleld is a gentleman, and I am personally proud that he belongs to the good old town of Warring- ton. I don't think that there is a man, woman or child in Warrington would say otherwise, and when the time does come I feel sure the election in Warrington will be fought with two gentlemen in the persons of Mr. Robert Pierpoint and Mr. Crosfield. but do please. my dear" Free Critic," withdraw the "able politician to boot." Kind regards, "Free Critic," and he advised if you want to do your cause any good in Warrington, don't write to the paper.—Thanking you, Hr. Editor, for your kindness, I am yours truly, "A HIGHER CRITIC." Warrington, 2lth September, 1605. The Water Committee and the Lawson Contract.

Sir,—At the Ratepayers' meeting unon this important subject. held in the Parr Hall on the 14th inst, some astounding revelations were made regarding the ways of the Water Committee and its legal adviser, the Town Clerk. It was stated on the 21st of September, 1900, five years ago, a contract was made with a Mr. Lawson for additional Waterworks at a cost of £24,000: that for the execution of the job the coutractor had tendered :IBM for £57,285; that up to February of this year the Water Engineer had signed certificates for £39,183 12s. 6d. • that £35,484 had actually been paid ; and that, to avoid litigation, the Town Clerk was en- deavonring to effect a friendly settlement of the balance with Mr. Lawson. And what must have been the astonishment of the assembled ratepayers when they were further told that there was not a single member of the Committee or of the Corporation who had a heck on a single penny of the amount :" and that no explanation was forthcoming, from any quarter, as to how the contract price had been exceeded by C 34,000 ! TI the allegations made at the meeting were in order, and I have no reason to doubt them, they reveal a state of laxity and incompetence probably without a parallel in municipal history. And if the other Committees of the Conncil conduct their business on the same lines as the Water Committee do the bankruptcy of the Cor- poration will only be a matter of time. Now the wiestionarises,how will the ratepayers, who are the masters of the Corporatian, deal with the dis- creditable and alarming situation thus brought to light? Will they content themselves by uttering some strong expressions of their disapproval, and then quietly sit down and allow the incapables to go on with their muddling to the scandal of the town and the shameful squandering of its resources ? The good government of the Borough and the flanncial interests of its inhabitants demand a very different policy. Gradually, as the November elections come round, the Council Chamber must be cleared of the crude men whose lack of experience renders then, wholly unfit to manage the large, and often complicated, transactions of the Corporation of an important town. The Alder- manic bench, too which in its humble way is so prone to imitate the obstructive manceuvres of "the lords " menet be relegated to their proper place in private life. Next to a seat in Parliament, a seat at the Council Board is the highest honour which the people can confer on a fallow citizen, and the recipients of this honour should be educated men of good standing, irreproachable in character, well versed in accounts. having no connection either directly or indirectly with the liquor traffic and sufficiently mg:a:tinted with municipal law to be independent of the dictation of the permanent officials whose duty is to obey, and not instruct, their superiors. And withal, men too honest and too honotintbie to prostitute their trust for personal gain. In their selec- tion, too, the abominable tricks of political bigotry should have no place, but the fair fame and prosperity of the town should be the ruling motives. Surely it ought not to be difficult to find thirty-six men answer- ing this description in a large town like Warrington. When our local parliament has been reformed by the excision of the windbags and amateurs who now stultify its proceedings, and the introduction of the type of men I have indicated an improved state of things will soon manifest itself. The various COM- mittees will understand and perform their duties ; the Town Clerk will ho relieved of general managership; and the income of the Corporation will bo rigidly con- fined to Corporation purposes. and none of it thrown away on the glorification of football or other institu- tions known to be accompanied by gambling and drunkenness. And, moreover, the cruel and selfish system which prevails elsewhere of employing labourers at starvation wages will be copied no loneer, but a more jnst and generous policy will prevail.—Yours truly TON A. September, 1005. _

div.head: NOVEMBER ELECTIONS. Probable Contests.
div.p: THE NOVEMBER ELECTIONS. Probable Contests.
7 =teen days.

There is every indication that at thelcovember elec- lions the electors in the majority of the wards in the town will be called upon to exercise their votes in the selection of municipal representatives. Present indi- cation:4 are that with one exception, the retiring Coun- cillors will seek an expression of the continued confi- dence of the burgesses. The Liberal party are already -.displaying considerable activity, and a number or ward meetings have been beld. A meeting of the Howley Ward Liberal Committee was held on Wednesday night Councillor Clegg presided ftnd there were also present Alderman Tinuion, Councillor Evans, Mr. J. Morton, and Mr. J. Howes, init. It was resolved unanimously to contest the Ward and several names were submitted It was decided to ask Mr, E. Pickavance to allow him- self to be nominated. Mr. E. Pickarance has signified his acceptance of the -invitation.

SUNDAY GAMIMING AT WARRINGTON. At Warrington on Monday, John Floyd, 26, street, George Jones, 215, Winwick-road, Richard Buckley, 30, Warburton-street, and Samuel Dickinson, 13,3ockey-street,were charged with gambling in Siddall- street on Sunday the 17th inst. The Chief Constable said the game the defendants were playing was a form .nt gambling rarely seen except in the lower rings of a racecourse, called • crown and anchor." The defendants were seen by Detective Clough playing the game, and the neighbourhood was a regular pitch for Sunday gamblers.—The Chairman (Alderman Bolton) said they -were determined to put down Sunday gambling ; and i Floyd was lined 2.05. and costs or one month, and the three defendants wore tined 10s. and costs or

There was little hope of success at Wigan in the breasts of the Warrington supporters, especially with such men as Fish, Hookenhall, Shugars, Naylor and Dickinson absent, but the players doing duty evidently had rosier views on the matter. Anyhow, I hove to compliment them on making a very good fight and succumbing only to misfortune. They started off in a' fashion which' frightened the Wigan folk. For once in a way there seemed to be unania.ity among the forwards and all pushed at once. Consequently They metaphorically moved the Wigan eight off the earth. At any rate they secured the ball five times out of six and within a quarter of an hour were a try ahead, Kenyon open- ing his account for the season in determined style. ' Unluckily the ccount had very soon to be closed as ' the fair-haired wing man sustained a damaged shoulder five minutes later which put him out of action for the rest of the day. Even then, the War- rington men did not lose heart and should have scored again if Harris had been anything of a dodger when challenged by Mason on the line. At half time they still lead by a try.

It is no use elaborating matters mach farther, as the brightest side of the picture has been shown. Wigan "bucked up" to some purpose on resuming and got the upper hand of Warrington's seven doughty forwards, who had been struggling against odds for a loag, time .1. Thomas, Lowe, and Latham scored tries and Mason kicked a goal, so that the Wirepullers had nothing to pall bet long faces at the close. They were not so badly beaten as I. would suggest. Lowe's try was a gift, for Hallam was impeded by two of his own I forwards, and the alleged flier had a clear course. Nevertheless, Thomas nearly caught him. The last try, Skipper Latham deserved full credit for. By the way he was not thought good enough for • Warrington once when his transfer foe stood at £7O. He would be well worth it now !

The game was a particularly open one and gave Referee Smith all the running about that he likes. There was passing galore on both sides, but a sad want of a Bob Wilson to pull it straight. Wigan tossed the ball all ways, and the combination was too erratic to be effective, though it provided plenty of speedy running for the spectators to cheer at. Jordan made a vary creditable debut on the Warrington side, and was always aggressive, while the halves were smart when they were getting the ball. Davies has a good deal of cleverness and he got the ball away to Harris twice in a fahion which would have meant points had Fish been the wing man. On the Wig in side, the star artiste was Anderson whose bare legs seemed to be everywhere, He took a lot of holding, and was well supported by Thomas,who has improved a lot. Mason was safe as the bank and compared well with Hallam. A word of praise is due to G. Thomas for the able way in which he filled Kenyon's vacant position. It can be said of him that he never made an error on the defence, and only lacked pace on the attack.
The points are two for a win and one for a draw. The percentage is calculated upon the basis of the total points possible.

There was mach satisfaction at Wigan when the A " team half-time score arrived. Secretary Taylor wore quite a " I told you so "look when he opened the telegram and found the Combination Champions two points down. The final chortle' fell to Warrington, however, for they pulled off the event in gallant fashion by '5 points to 2, though poorly represented. Knight played finely on the defence, but the forwards were very weak in the packs.

Only a small proportion of the huge crowd at the football match went over to Sprin;lield Park to see the SO yards sprint between jack Fish and !lucky Green. Sixpence seems rather a lot to pay for Bor 9 seconds sport, and only about 1200 paid it. The Warringion man was a favourite all round, and when the pistol cracked he inade short work of (keen, and broke the tap 3 a clear 3 yards in front. He seemed to travel remarkably fast, and the time 8 2-5 was pretty warm, considering he was not pushed in any , way. Let us hope he will show as .019 n a pair of heels to the Halifax men to-day. -- Warrington expect to have a stronger team at Halifax to-day than Tast week, and hopes are high that the handsome victory of last season may be repeated. Fish returns to the left wing, in place of Kenyon, which is the only change in the three-quarter line Hockenhall displaces (Davies at half-back, but the forwards remain the same, Sbugars and Naylor being still unlit. The latter is suffering from quinzy. The full team should be therefore Hallamu, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Jordan and Harris, threequarters ; 1 Brooks and Hockenhall, half-backs ; Boardman, Preston, Thomas. Bowling. The bowling season is now nearing the end and the concluding stages have witnessed some interesting com- petition. On the 16th inst the contest for the prize of £5 given by Mr. E. England was decided over the Corporation green in Victoria Park. The competition was not that success which it deserved to be. Unfor- tunately it clashed with the final rounds of the Works individual main and many men who would otherwise have entered were prevented from doing so, owing to the prior engagement. As a result only 22 players turned out but what was lacking in numbers was made up by the excellence of the bowling. Other prizes I were offered and the winners were placed as follows : 1, T. Ellison ; 2, H. Clare ; 3, J. Roberts ; 4, T. Dunn, 5. J. Hall ; 6, R. Fairbrother ; 7, W. Barton and 8, J. Unswortb. div.p: WARRINGTON BRITISH SCHOOLS.

The distribution of prizes took place at the above school on Wednesday evening. Mr. A. J. Jolley pre- sided and there were also present—the Rev. J. tone, Councillor Fulton Smith, Mr. J. Moore Murray, Mr. Ed. Wallington. and Mr. S. W. Jeffery. The Rev. J. YONGE congratulated the teachers upon the success of the school and the prize winners, not upon the value of the prizes they had won, but upon having proved themselves deserving of prizes. The years of youth were not years to he wasted in mirth , and enjoyment bat years full of golden and glorious opportunity which if faithfully employed would fit them for success in after life. fie co7anselled them earnestly to maka,f all use of their opportunities for acquiring knowledge and to cultivate stronglya love for good books. They must not seek all their recreation in sport. They could quite properly and usefully seek a great deal of it in that way, but by reading they must cultivate as much as was possible an ever fextending ! knowledge, and so be able to form broad and liberal views upon things in general. They must cultivate ! resolution, and make a deliberate decision for a good ' and great aim in life. If they kept on trying they were bound to succeed. (Applause). div.head: JUNIOR LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: JUNIOR LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
A New grganization for Warrington.

A successful meeting was held on Tuesday evening in the large room at the Libetal Club for the purpose of inaugurating a Junior Liberal Association. The meeting was well attended and it was unanimously ! decided to form an Association. The following ' officers were elected to act for the first ' three months : —President, 11fr. J. Howes ; Vice-presidents,Messrs. E. Osborne and A.H.Sanders; treasurer, Mr. E. Osborne; secretary, Mr. Harold Gray • with a 'committee of eleven. ,It was decided to hold ;he meetings weekly for the purpose of discuss- ing political questions. The first meeting will take place on Monday next when Mr. J. Howes will deliver an address on the origin and history of the two political parties. 4. An interesting discussion took place concerning the work of the Association and great entnusiasin prevailed.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH WESLEYANISM. Two Days' Bazaar at Bold-street School.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH WESLEYANISM. Two Days' Bazaar at Bold-street School.

r The new Wesleyan Methodist Church at Stockton Heath is nearing completion, and when the building is opened it will form a handsome addition to the architec- tural features of the district. The flotation of the I scheme has naturally involved heavy expenditure, but funds have been contributed with welcome celerity, and prior to Wednesday there remained only a debit balance lof £7OO. With the object of reducing this suns to the extent of £3OO a bazaar has been held on Wednesday ' and Thursday in the Bold-street schools. The proceed- , jugs were opened on Wednesday by Mrs. James Dodds,in the presence of a large assembly. Mr. W. H.Sherburn pre- sided and there were also present :—the Revs. S. Pitt, William Mellor, J. Manning, A. C. Parker, J. Yont,m, J. F. Matthews, Messrs. P. Stringer, S. Moss, P. Silcock, F. Pendlebury, G. Whitfield, Mrs. J. G. Withinshaw, Mrs. Ziba Armitage, and Mrs. J. Yonge. the C/fArrot kx at the outset explained that be pre- sided in the absence of Mr. Richardson who was pre- vented by illness from being present. When he (Mr. Sherburn) first came to know the Wesleyan Church at Stockton Heath, it was a little place with one room which was used for services, Sunday school and all purposes. When they tackled the new scheme some of them were afraid they would not be able to carry it through, but the majority looked upon it as worth trying. They had succeeded but not without assistance from other Free Churches —assistance which had been generously given. The people of Stockton Heath had worked hard and he hoped that in the future instead of having to record an adverse balance at every quarterly meeting thee would be able to report. a balance in hand. (Applause). Mr. PENDIABLII:LY presented a brief financial state- ment. The new church including all extras would cost £1.719, to which had to be added £125 mortage on the old building. Amounts received and promised totalled £9Ol Os. 101, so that, there remained a balance of £759 still to be raised. (Applause). Mrs. Doom said she was pleased to be present and congratulate them upon getting their new chapel.which, though she had not seen it., she heard was very beautiful. She thought they asPlethodists had been slow to realize one thing in regard to their places of worship which was that a thing of beauty was a .ioy for over. So far as Stockton Heath was concerned they would have that joy. She did not think that alone would content them. The Psalmist had said his one desire was that he "might dwell in the house of the Lord and behold the beauty of the Lord." If their sanctuary was tilled with that spirit the iniluence and power which would go out from it would be far reaching and many would bless it. They were mot there to help their Stockton Heath friends who, she hoped, would be encouraged by the generous re3ponse to their appeal.Sh had great pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause). ! Mr. Moss proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Dodds for her services. They were greatly indebted to Mr. and Mrs. Dodds for their substantial contributions towards the work and for their sympathy. (Applause.) Mr. R. Mmr.nu. seconded. The Rev. JOHN YoKGE supported. He was glad to have that opportunity of cordially wishing them well. Ile trusted the new church %wild be one of growing prosperity (Applause,) The vote was heartily accorded; Mr. Dorms briefly returning thanks. The Chairman was heartily Caulked on the motion of the Rev. S: PITT. - - .

- The roona had bean beautifully &aerated for the occasion, and the stalls, which were laden with a variety of articles, were in charge of the following : Fancy Stall, Mesdames Moss, Pendlebury,S. H. Gerrard; dairy fruit and produce stall, Messrs. S.Moss, .1. Miller, P. Stringer, R. Miller, H. Brereton; refrestment stall and tea rooms, Mesdames Sherburne, Woodward, Towe, Hughes, Dann and Rawbottorn, and the Misses A. Woodward, Barlow, Sherburne, Hall and Neilson. Wednesday's proceedings were not so successful as it was honed they would be the sum of £7O only being realised. THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

Thurday's opening ceremony was well attended. Mr. James Dodds presided and there were also present The Revs. NV. Mellor, J. Gunnell and J. Manning, Mrs. Dodds, Mrs. J. G. Withinshaw, Messrs. S. Moss, R. J. Moss, P. Stringer, G. Weaver, and F. Pendlebory. The CHAIRMAN in asking Mrs. Withinshaw to open the bazaar, said no one bad a stronger sympathy with the work which was being done in Stockton Heath than she had. He had long felt the need for a Wesleyan Chapel at Stockton Heath and he was glad to be present that afternoon to wish God-speed to Mr. Moss and his co-adjutors in the work which they had undertaken. He congratulated the Stockton fleath Wesleyans upon the success which had already attended their efforts, and wished them a full and early fruition of their desire. (Applause). Mrs. WITHINSHAW said Mr. Withinshaw and she had the scheme at heart and took a deep interest in the pro- gress of the work at Stockton Heath and the little they had been able to do had been done very willingly. Mr. Withinshaw fully recognized the need for the new church and rejoiced upon the approaching completion of the work. She had the greatest pleasure in declaring the sale open and in wishing it every success. (Applause). Mr. P. STRINGER proposed a vote of thanks to MTS. Withinshaw and Mrs. Dodds for their services. Mr. P. J. Moss seconded. One of the most encourag- ing things connected with the Work was the generous response which had been made by other churches in the circuit to the appeal for assistance. (Applause.) I The Rev. Wq,LtaNt 111ELLort in supporting. said the new building would be a very tasteful one and he was , glad it was not like so many of their chapels, the [erectors of which thought that four walls and a roof were all that was necessary. Mr. MELLOR announced that Mr. Dodds had handed a cheque for £lO to the treasurer. (Applause.) The vote was heartily carried. The proceedings on each day were rendered addition- ally attractive hv musical items which were contributed by Miss Lloyd Williams juvenile orchestra, the children from Stockton Heath who had been trained by Mrs. Woodward. Mr. Edward Pearce, Mr. X. Griffiths, Miss Cox,Miss Pitt, Mr. D. J. Corrin, Mr, O. Gough, and Mr Woodhead.

div.head: MAYORALTY,
div.p: THE MAYORALTY,
Alderman Bolton Accepts Office for a Third Year. . _

Alderman Boltnn-17,a—t the invitation of the Town Council,intimated his II to accept the office of Mayor for a third year. The matter ,was under consider- ation at a caucus meeting of the Town Council held at the, Town Hall on Monday night. There were several propositions, the names mentioned being the' present Mayor (Alderman William Bolton), Alderman Pier- point, Alderman Smethurst, Mr. F. Monks, and Mr. C. E. Parker. Eventually it was resolved that Alderman Bolton be asked to continue in office for a third year, and a deputation consisting of Aldermen Fiiirclour,h Fran- comb , and Smethurst waited upon him. Alderman Bolton expressed his willingness to again accept office, provided he had the support of the Council.

div.head: LOCAL EVENING SCHOOLS.
div.p: LOCAL EVENING SCHOOLS.
DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES.I

rDuring the week the prizes and certificates, gained by the students attending the various evening continuation schools held inithe town last winter, have been distri- buted. On Monday evening Alderman Bennett, chair- ' man of the Education Committee attended at Fairfield j schools for this purpose. The chair was occupied by the j Rector and amongst other also present were Councillor Craik, Colonel Buckton, Mr. T. May, Mr. J. Moore j I Murray (director of education) and Miss Taylor (head- mistress). The CHAIRMAN expressed his pleasure at seeing so large an attendance of students. He emphasised the importance of a regular attendance at the evening , J classes and especially of the girls making themselves I 'proficient in cooking and needlework. (Applause). Alderman BKNNETr remarked that the attendance at the evening school last winter was not by any means; satisfactory. At the beginning of the session 100 chil- dren entered their names but towards the end of the term the number had dwindled to 25. That could not by any stretch of the imagination be regarded as satis- factory. That year they had begun well, but it was necessary that they should continue in well being and attend the classes regularly. The importance of a good education could not be over estimated. Every day and hour of their lives fresh sources of know- ledge would open out and they would have the opportunity of acquiring that which would make them good citizens. In those evening , schools he understood that amongst other subjects they ' were taught domestic economy and sowing and the extreme importance of their attending to ;hose sub- jects and mastering them meant a great deal to them and those associated with them in after life. How- ever much they learnt they should always remember that there were greater things to learn and those sub- jects which they mastered should encourage them to climb higher and higher. He hoped the evening classes would be a great success during the coming session. , (Applause.) Alderman BENNETT distributed the prizes as follows : —Eva Jackson. umbrella; Margaret Malone. work box; Lily Proffitt, books ; Alice Wilkinson and Ada Wilkin- son, work boxes ; Ellen Boast and Sarah Cartwright, books and certificates in domestic economy; Annie Rathbone, umbrella and certificate in domestic economy. Colonel BUCKTON moved a vote of thanks to the Rector and Alderman Bennent for their services.

Councillor CR UK seconded. In his opinion, he said, before long it would not be optional for boys and girls to attend evening schools, but it would be made compulsory. He hoped the students present would not require any compulsion, but that they would continue to attend the classes throughout the whole of the session. (Applause). The vote was heartily accorded, cheers being given for the Rector and Alderman Bennett.
Both gentlemen having briefly replied the proceedings terminated.
AT HAMILTON•STREET SCHOOLS.

Later in the evening Alderman Bennett attended at Hamilton-street schools for the purpose of distributing the prizes. The Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson pre- sided and there were also present : Mr. Thomas May, Mr. J. Moore Murray, Mr. F. H.Longshaw (headmaster) Miss Timewell and Miss Barker.

The Cll.l rum AN said he was very glad indeed to see such a'good muster of students at the beginning of the season. He wondered how many of them would continue to attend until the end of the session, because his exper- ience of night schools had been that as the term advanced the number of students diminished. Ile did not know the reason for that but whatever the reason it was not a good one. They would never getany good out of a thing which they begun and left unfinished and therefore he hoped they would be able to maintain the excellent record of attendance which they had that night. (Applause.) Alderman 13zNNErr said that figures which had been given to him with reference to past sessions made him rather discourt enthusiasm which the students displayed that night, as they showed that the number of students I decreased as the session advanced. Anything which was worth doing %vas worth doing well and if they were to succeed in life they must take the fullest advantage of the teaching which they were able to get in those evening schools. The one essential factor of success in life was a good education. He did not wish them to think that by success he meant the accumulation of wealth, but he meant that success which would make them good citizens, and for which they required a good education. He would be the last in the world to advo- cate that they should have no pleasure. They most cultivate the bodies as well as the mind hat they must not think the sole object in life was to attend football matches or become good players. As a duty to them- selves they must make the best of the faculties with which they had been endowed by cultivatln,g and developing them to the fullest extent. (Applause). Alderman BENNETT then amidst appianse distributed the prizes, the winners of which were :—John Robinson, John E. Peguna, James W. Johnson, Thomas H. Greg- son, and Edward Carroll, certificates in arithmetic; Harold Plinston, and Charles E. Walker, scholarships to the Technical Institute; John Bretherton, Joseph Chatterton. Samuel Hayes, John W. Hudson Thomas Massey,and Joseph Bennett, scholarships to the Techni- cal Institute, and certificates in arithmetic ; James Sudell, Joseph Bailey, John Grundy, Samuel Lomas,and Herbert Rigby, books • Gecrge Hall, Edmund Bothwell, Frank Hackett, Stanley Gleave, and Mozart Wilcock, books, and certificates in arithmetic.
Mr. MAI' moved a vote of thanks to Canon Steven- son and Alderman Bennett for their services, urging upon the students the necessity of their striving to mount the educational ladder.

The vote was heartily carried, cheers being given for both gentlemen. Alderman BENKETIC briefly returned thanks. Mr. LONGS-HAW, on behalf of the teaching staff expressed his thanks to Alderman Bennett and the Chai- rman for their presence. A brief reply by Canon Stevemon brought tho pro- coAings to an end. HEATHS-EDE SCHOOLS,

Col.l3CiliOr FULTON-SMITII distributed the prizes at Heathsida schools on Tuesday evening. 1 The Rev. W. Bracecarnp presided and arnonrrst other present were— Messrs. J. H. Smethurst, T. May, J. Moore Murray (director of education), and T. Rddon (superintendent of the school).

The CliAtint.l.NT wanted till bays to remember that when-they left school that, had not finished their educa- tion. Only educated lads would be able to take important positions in life. Councillor FULTON SNIITH said the future depended upon the boys of the present generation. A tremendous responsibility rested upon the teachers, but there was also a great resnousibility which rested upon the boys themselves. Whatever they learnt they must learn thoroughly. Whatever they studied they must master, and they could only do so by adopting a systematic way of working. He strongly advised them not to read the scrappy magazines which were published, but to take up good books and master them. Councillor FutiroN-SAt frit then distributed the prizes as follows :—Fred Waywell, Joseph Price, William Jolley, John If. Grainger, William Ashbrook. and Reginald B. Dixon, certificates in arithmetic ; Sydney T. Ince, Samuel Jones, Arthur Makin, Harry Shaw, and Ernest F. Baker. Scholarships to the Technical Institute; Willliam Battersby, Harry Mason. John E. Pardoe. Alfred Whitehouse, and Clifton Billington, scholar- ships to the technical institute, and certificates in arithmetic; Arthur Blease, William Denton, and Joseph Lloyd,books ; William Mannion, Albert Way- well, Edward Lowe, Frederick W. Bennett, Bernard Williams, and Arthur Brobbin, Ernest Bennett, and William J. Holden, books and certificates in arithmetic. Mr. ALIY moved a vote of thanks to Councillor Fulton Smith and the Chairman for their services. Mr. J. H. SIIETIIIIRST seconded. The vote was accorded with enthusiasm, hearty cheers being given by the boys. A vote of thanks was accerded to Mr. Eddon and the teaching staff. _ _

EDDEN, ill responding, said that on the whole the work in the school was very satisfactory. Nine out of every ten of the boys attended the school to work, and he urged the students to attend regularly throughout the session. Mr.J. Mooa t 1 SiSAveraphasiserl the necessity of the lads studying while they were at school. As an example of sport and study could he combine he instanced Mr. C. B. Fry,who he said was first in all sports and first in school life and college examination.' (Applause.) Mr. Fry did not play cricket and then 'waste all his time talking about, it until the next match came round, but went on with other pursuits ard so got proficient in them all. They should remember that ten minutes' actual work was worth an hour's.tinkering at study, and that whatever was worth doing was worth doing well. (Applause.)

div.head: MOTOR-CAR FATALITY. --- Warrington Child's Tragic End.
div.p: MOTOR-CAR FATALITY. --- Warrington Child's Tragic End.
"A PURE ACCIDENT."

Winwick-street was on Tuesday evening the scene of the first motor-car fatality which has happened in Warrington and the sad event naturally created a painful sensation. It appears that at half-past five a 30 horse-power car belonging to Ur. Arthur Entwistle, of Roy House, Albert road, Bolton, was being driven out of the town by way of Winwick-street, by Ernest sari% chauffeur. Eye-witnesses state that it was travelling at about four miles an hour and that the chauffeur was exercising every cantion,in fact a police officeir. remarked to a friend that if all drivers were as careful there would be fewer accidents. When the , car reached the Central Station the street was in a congested state. The chaffeur was steering the car past a lurry when a child named Sarah Ann Lawless, aged: twelve, 47, Orford-street, who had been sent on an errand, suddenly left the footpath. The driver sounded his h9rn, but the child became confused and was caught by the mudguard of the car and knocked down. One of the front wheels passed over her and she was so seriously injured about the head as to be at once rendered insensible. The car was immediately , stopped and the child was conveyed in it to the ! Infirmary where she died a few minutes after adinis- sion. Mr. Entwistle, vita was riding in the car, reported the accident to the police. He was naturally very much distressed by the fatality.
THE INQUEST. DRIVER EXONERATED FROM BLAME.

----- Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held the inquest at the Police Station on Wednesday afternoon.—Mr. M. Fielding, solicitor, Bolton, appeared on behalf of Mr. Entwistle who was also present in Court. Joseph Lawless, stationary engine driver, 19, Orford street, deceased's father, said he last saw the child alive shortly before five o'clock on Tuesday evening. Almost immediately afterwards he left home to go to work,and a little later his wife sent deceased on an errand to a shop in Winwick street. Witness saw the child lying dead at the Infirmary at 9 o'clock. Ernest Surr, chauffeur employed by Mr. Arthur Entwistle, stated that he was driving the car at the rate of about four miles an hour. He was on the right hand side passing a lorry and a cyclist when he saw the deceased leave the footpath about five yards in front of the car and attempt to cross the road. He sounded the horn and ?deceased turned round and made for the footpath. Suddenly, however, she turned again and tried to cross the road, but the near mud guard of the car caught her and knocked her down. He at once stopped the car and with assistance picked the deceased up and conveyed her to the Infirmary. After- wards he drove to the police °lice and reported the matter.

In reply to the Coroner witness stated that Mr. Entwistle's son was sitting at the front of the car with him. Mr. Entwistle, another son, a daughter and a little child were sitting behind. The car was a3O horse power machine with four speeds and reverse. It was going at between four and six miles an hour, and witness pulled up in the length of the car. Questioned by the Chief Constable, witness stated that he had been a chauffeur ever since the Act came into operation. His licence had been endorsed once. Mr. Fielding explained the circumstances of this case, pointing out that Slur was only driving at seven miles an hour, but as Mr. Entwistle would not com- pensate a man with whose vehicle be accidently collided, a prosecution was instituted. Mr. Entwistle had sufficient confidence in Surr to retain his services as he considered he was not altogether to blame. Charles Cunningham, attendant at , the County Asylum, Winwick, who was cycling in Winwick-street gavela similar version of the accident. In his opinion the car was being driven at about four miles an hour. ilt was pulled up n about seven yards. Witness thought the chauffeur did everything he could to avoid the accident.
A forge labourer, named Hamilton, 33, Plumpton- street, also described the fatality, and said the cAr was not travelling at more than five or six miles an hour.

P.C. Dennett, acting Coroner's officer, stated that he was standing in Horsernarket-street a few minutes before five when he saw Mr. Entwistle's car proceeding at not more than between four and five miles an hour. He watched the car till it reached the end of Scotland- road. He remarked ton friend that if every driver took such precautions there would be fewer accidents. The Coroner, in summing up, said he was not going to assume that the jury had any unfair antipathy to motor cars and drivers, but that they would view the matter in a sensible light. The same law applied to motor cars as applied to other vehicles, and it was only incumbent upon drivers to exercise reasonable care, skill and judgment. The jury found that the fatality was a pure accident and exonerated the chAeur from all blame.

Mr. Fielding expressed Nil.. Entwistle' deep regret at the accident. Ile sympathised sincerely with the parents and would be prepared to pay the funeral expenses and make every recompense he could. The Coroner expressed appreciation of the way in which Mr. Entwistle had acted in the matter.
Mr. Entwistle was obi-O-Q1;-n-iu-C-1;iffs-t7e;s-ed by the fatality, and burst into tears on leaving the court.

div.head: EXTENSIONS AT M ESSRS. CROSFIELD'S. An Island Extension--More
div.p: EXTENSIONS AT M ESSRS. CROSFIELD'S. An Island Extension--More

Employment. A number of veryhopeful signs, all indicating the approach of a healthy revival in our great local industries, have recently been noted and it is very gratifying to publish an announcement which shows that Messrs J. Crosfield and Sons are still maintaining that steady progress which has characterized their operations even in times of general depression. For some years the growing demands of their busi- ness and the increasing difficulty of obtaining land on this side of the river, have hampered the firm's opera- tions. The directors have now decided to use for exten- sions land on the other side, and for this purpose have acquired about 45 acres in Lower Walton on the tongue of land enclosed opposite their works by the bend in the river. The plot thus acquired will be cut off by the new channel of the Ship Canal Co., and will thus, except for the causeway projected in connection with that scheme, be completely insulated by water. Here they will provide the much needed extra!accom modation for their ordinary work, and will probably before loAg make a now departure which will, they hope, furnish work for a large number of additional hands. _

To connect their main factory with this island annexe a bridge will be constructed at considerable cost opposite the warehouse, where the river is 200 ft. in width. This bridge will, by agreement with the NferseyCoaservanry, be of the same height as Runcorn Bridge, 751 t. above high water mark, and will be used not, only as a me,' ns of communicationlfor passengers, but to convey various liquids by pipes and to carry electric power lines. A tunnel scheme has been seriously considered for this purpose, but in view of the unfortunate experience of the contractors at Fiddler's Ferry, the directors decided in favour of a bridge. Nor does the enterprise end here, for it is the com- pany's intention ultimately to erect, near the site of the bridge and on the other side, a jetty for loading and discharging its numerous steamers. The plans for the new works are fully elaborated and work will, we are informed, be started as soon as the pipe line conveyor is in position. It is pleasant further to be able to say,on the authority of the Managing Director, that lsfessrs. Crostield and and Sons have happily not suffered from any of the recent crises in the trade. The firm is fully occupied in every department, and the prospects of this continu- ing so are of the best.

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
WEEK ENDING SEPTEMBER 23rd, 1905,
During tho 'Week, the following births and deaths were registered :—Warrington Registration District births, 55, deaths, O. The excess of births over deaths was 35. _

The birth-rate was equal to -41.3 The death-rate from all causes was equal to 15•0 per 1,000 against 180 the average of the previous 4 weeki and against 211 the corresponding period of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymotio diseases NIUS equal to 37 per 1,000, against 57 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks and against 10.6 the corresponding period of 1904. The ages of mortality were:- 0--4 1-5 5-15 15-25 23-35 65—up. Total It 1 1 5 2 20. The deaths included-1 from measles, 1 from whoop- ing cough, 3 from diarrlaceit, 1 from puerperal fever, 1 from phthisis, 1 from other tubercular diseases, 1 from ' cancer' 1 from lung diseases, 9 from all other causes. The following caset of infections diseases have been reported during the week :—Scarlet fever, 1 case, phthisis, 2 cases. Total number of patients in hospital, week ending 23rd September, 1905, 36 ; Newton 24. Rural District, 2: Borough, 10. METEOROLOGY.—The mean temperature was St Fah. and therefore the same Rs the preceding week. The maximum temperature 63F., was recorded on the 17th inst., and the minimum temperature 36F., on the 20th inst. _
The ntinfall measured .08 inch. The general direction was S.E.
J. GUEST GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Missionary Sermons. Sermons in aid of the Medical Missionary work carried on under the Church Missionary Society were preached in St. Paul's Church on Sunday by the Rev. W. R. Cole, Medical Association Secretary for the North-West of England. Interesting information was given by the preacher- In some parts of the wide field of operations new hospitals were beine built,and others would soon be required. The hospitals were always equipped as efficiently as possible, and were constantly winning high praise from distinguished visitors. St. John's Presbyterian Church. The annual harvest thanksgiving services were held at St. John's on Sunday, the Rev. J. L. Milne, 8.D., minister of the church, preaching morning and evening. There was a good attendance at each service. In the evening the preacher chose for his text Deuteronomy, c. 12. v. 10 to 12, where Moses described Palestine as a land which "God careth for." Mr. Milne pointed out how, in many respects, their own land with its uncertain i climate resembled that of Palestine, and taught men to think of Cod. In the towns, where they did not so directly depend upon harvests, they were apt to forget God and not to feel their dependence upon him, there- ! fore it was well that they should have those harvest ; thanksgivings to remind them of God's continued good- I ness to them. The choir sang the anthem "Clap your bands oh ye people I" Mr. J. W. Jewett Presided at the organ. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. Sunday last was prize day in connection with this very prosperous Society, when 363 books were distribe Ited, making the total distributed since the society's formation, 11,012, which must have a very beneficial effect upon the minds and lives of the men. Mr. E. S. A. Robson presided, and spoke upon " The perfect Man- hood," while Mr. E. A. Pickering, of Liverpool, dealt with" Moral courage." Mr. F. Brown sang The river of years" in good style. Mr. Bentley, of Newton Heath, and Mr. S. Rowlands took part in the meeting. Six new members were heartily welcomed, making a total of 516. Mr. Payton presided at the organ. I An open meeting of the Society was held the previous 'Sunday, when there was a large gathering. Mr. B. 1-Farrar presided, and said he was pleased to have the Iplensure of the presence of the Wycliffe choir, and he gave them and Mr. Power, the principal speaker, all the time he could. Mr. Power touched upon incidents of , his work in Manchester amongst the paor, giving some beautiful examples of love and self-denial for the sake of others. His address was listened to with great attention and sympathy. The choir WAS in splendid form, and delighted the meeting with expressive renderings of " Sing to the iLord of harvest " and "The radiant morn." The Chairman referred to , the presence there of old friends and supporters a the P.S.A. movement, Mr. and Mrs. J. Podmore, who had just celebrated their golden wedd- ing. He expressed the congratulations of the meeting to them, and said he hoped they would be spared many ! more happy years. Mr. W 13eswick and Mr. C. Eccles also took part in the meeting. Six new members were heartily welcomed, making a total of 510. The choir was under the leadership of/ %fr. %V. H. Payton. A colleAion in aid of the fund of the Society was taken Civic Purity and the Civic Conscience. Sermon by the Rev. J. F. Matthews. " Serious Lowering of Public ideals." The Rev. J. F. Matthews preached on the above subject at Latchford Baptist Church on Sunday evening. { The civic conscience, he said, was the name for the sensitiveness of public opinion to moral and religious , ideals, and as these were raised, so purity in the munici- pality and in the State would largely increase. No ' man, in reading the prophetic literature of the Bible, could escape concluding that the greatest burden the I prophets had to carry was the fateful declension of public morals, the lack of purity in public life. The picture painted by Second Isaiah was indeed tragic, and involved what eventually took place, the complete and final disintegration of Jewish national unity. It was ' always a perilous thing for a nation or a municipality to disregard the moral aspect of its life. Turning to modern times, the preacher said that during the last ten years the country, as a whole, had witnessed a serious lowering of its public ideals. Conscience was sneered at. The South African millionaire had won all round, and to-day the hateful sight was witnessed of Chinese slaves, whipped, tortured, lined and imprisoned for revolting against the fraud and deception of which they were the dupes. All this took place under the British flag, in his name and theirs. British honour had ceased to be. The British name was tarnished, stained aud dragged in the dust by foul-hearted traitors. At home things were scarcely better. The education muddle was but a sign of the underlying moral obliquity of men in power. Further, in various municipalities where actual fraud, malversation of public funds, and dishoth•sty had not been practised, secrecy and dissimu- lation had created disquiet in the public mind. In our own town during five years past public opinion had been seriously disturbed, and heated controveries had not yet yet died down. Rightly or wrongly, suspicion had been aroused that all was not right. Surely this ,kind of thing ought not to be. Where was the remedy? The pulpit was a public preceptor, yet there were some who declared that such a subject as " Civic purity and a civic conscience" was not suitable for a pulpit dis- course, and did not come within the purview of the Gospel. Others said that unless the pulpit spoke out truthfully and boldly on current events, it was doomed to lose its influence. He asked what was the poor preacher to do? Speak the truth and fear not I The remedy lay with the Churches themselves. They ought to be the salt of public opinion. In their Master's name they ought neither to wink at, nor condone, nor tolerate anything in the Commonwealth that was detrimental to its best life, and its highest concerns. The Late Mr. R. G. Henshall Memorial Service at Latchford. There WAS a large congregation at Latchford Wes- leyan Church when an impressive memorial service to the late" Mr. R. G. Henshall, for many years manager of the Warrington Branch of the Liverpool and Dis- trict Bank, was held. At the conclusion of his sermon, which was founded on the words "He went about doing good," the Rev. J. Manning said that by the sudden death of Mr. R. G. Henshall they had lost one of their most valued helpers, whose place it would be exceed- ingly difficult to fill. Mr. Henshall was an example of the debt which the towns and cities of England owed to the villages of our land. The vitality and vigour of the towns were kept up by a constant inflow of some of the best life in the country. The villages and ham- lets had sent forth a very large proportion of those who occupied prominent positions in the municipal and religious life of the towns to-day. Mr. Henshall was an illustration of this. He was born on April 26th, 1349, in the quiet Cheshire village of Styal, and his early years were spent in a type of Christ:an home which, perhaps, . was not so common now as then. His father was a godly man of the stricter sort, a man of sterling worth and uprightness of character, who played a prominent part in the village life. Mr. Henshall was educated at the Stockport Grammar School, and, at the age of 16, through the influence of , Mr. George Crosfield, he entered the service of the ! Manchester and Liverpool District Bank. For 40 years, with one short break of three years at Haslingden, he remained at the Warrington Branch. By sheer merit land ability he worked his way up from the position of j junior clerk to that of manager. In 1873 he was ! ! appointed cashier, and in 183 e accountant. Seven I years later he was transferred to Haslingclen as branch I manager, balm only stayed there three years, for at the end of that time the post of manager of the War- rington Branch became vacant—through the death of Mr. William Barlow well-known in Methodist circles— and Mr. Henshall was promoted to the vacant place. The appointment proved in every way popular, and in his capable bands the business of the bank was doubled. , Very early in life he became a member of the Wesleyan I Methodist Church, and as a youth he began Christian I work as a Sunday school teacher at Styal and after- 1, wards at Warrington. For over forty years he served unsparingly the church of his choice. When the new schools were being built at Bold-street he walked many miles and spent runny days collecting money for that enterprise. For a time he sang in Bold-street ! choir. As the years passed he filled nearly { every office open to laymen in the Methodist Church. The debt they owed Ihim was very great. In the Master's service there were men with varying gifts. Some excelled in the more directly spiritual work and some in the business departments of the church. In the latter Mr. Henshall found a sphere for which he was pre-eminently fitted. His business train- ing and ability were at their service unreservedly. Perfect frankness was one of his chief characteristics, and though perhaps a few did not always appreciate his outspokenness, it was this very quality which led people to trust him. His frankness, however, was wedded to an innate kindness and geniality which won for him a great circle of friends. During the last' 11 years he had been a Fource of great strength to the Church, and his piece would be hard to fill.—At the conclusion of the service the Dead March in" Saul " was played on the organ by Miss Hartley.

And they, are the things for which the great Trade Union Leaders are conspicu- ous to-day."—The Labour Recant. * * I "Dr. Barnard° is dead, and the world is poorer for his passing. Many a man at home, and many more in that Greater Britain over-seas,one time wiafs, will drop a tear and think it no unmanly thing to do so in sorrow at his death."—" Guardian." * * The General Committee of the National Council of the Evangelical Free Churches has unanimously passed a resolution protesting against any future introduction of indentured Chinese coolies into South Africa awl urging that immediate steps should be taken for the gradual repatriation of those now in the Transvaal. So great has been the interest manifested in the utterances of Mr. R. L. Outhwaite on :Chinese Labour that the reports of his speeches at Parr Hall and the Co-operative Hall are being issued in pamphlet form- Copies will be available next week on application te Mr. J. Howes. iun.. at the Liberal Club,Bewsey street. * * * _ Alderman bolton has accepted an invitation from the caucus meeting of the Council to be Mayor for another year. Apparently it is becoming the custom for Warrington Mayors to hold office three years in succession, and we all know there is nothing harder ter break tnat custom. There is a sad lack of competition for a post of so much honour in the town. * * * A novel feature in the harvest decoration at St. John's, Blackpool, has attracted much attention at the services. A poor woman, unable to afford fruit flowers, or vegetables, but still anxious to give her mite, filled a bottle with water, and labelling it " Thank God for the rail'," sent it to the church, The viear, appreciating her good intention, gave it a prominent place amongst the decorations. * * A recent speech of the President of the Johannes- burg Chamber of Miners suggests that the mine- owners are not unwilling to see some of the China- men escape. There will be fewer to send home when the day for repatriation arrives. The conduct of the mine-owners has throughout been of the most sordidly faithless character and to eventually leave the Colony at the mercy of the Chinese would be quite within the scope of their villany. * * * Labouchere writes in " Truth " with accustonma incisiveness of the "No-Hat Movement," which be observed in great popularity the other Sunday among the cyclists going out of London. As the dust an suffocating, he thinks that it might well be rename the dirty head movement. "The other day," he adds, " it was a no-boot movement, the day before that a no-waistcoat movement. We shall probably bare next a no-shirt or a no-trousers mo--ement. The' might all be classed together as no-brain movements- * * A tribute from His Majesty's Inspector should be a feather in the cap of Warrington boys. Mr. Percival, who who has made frequent inspections of the. Warrington day schools, says that in Warrington be always tinds boys more courteous than in other towns' Here when they meet him in the- street they resper; fully touch their caps and say" Good morning, sir whereas in other places they are content to rec.ard , him with curiosity and exclaim " Hello ! there's °the, inspector." Warrington school boys may be pardonen if henceforth:they are a little conceited. *** Mr. T. O'Donnell, who delivered such a stirring address at the Irish demonstration, is known [lB " Kerry Gale." When he was returned to Parlia- ment ho greatly astounded that august assembly by delivering his maiden speech in-his native tongue. In respolidint, to a vote of thanks at Thursday's meet- ing he adopted the same novel course, much to the amazement of the majority at his hearers. Peoge have been speculating since as to whether part of "important announcement on the present political situation " was included in this mysterious speech-. The Tory Press looks upon the Analo-Japanese treaty as a stroke of genius by that-heaven-bora Statesman, Lord Lansdowne. Whether it is so is very open to doebt. As a consequence we may quite conceivably find ourselves embroiled with Germany or faced by a coalition of European powers, while the positive contempt for national opinion by the Govern- ment is to be unhesitatingly condemned. " Everrue knows " says the " Morning Leader " " what the authority of this Government is worth, and we unhesi- tatingly dispute its mdral right to make death-b,ed dispositions of the very highest Imperial interests. * Warrington has had its motor fatality, but the incident is not one which will add to the antipathy against motorists felt in many quarters. The chauffeur was driving with conspicuous care and had no possible means of averting the sad accident. When a child steps off the footpath in front of a moving vehicle nothing but luck can prevent a catastrophe. New. often does this sort of thing happen to the average cyclist ? Frequently ; and oftener than not nothing but the agility of the rider saves the careless Pede,s- trian. In this sad affair no blame is attached anyone, and both the bereaved and the motorist, ar°' be sympathised with. t-sie * * The din of battle is almost audible already, though the elections are a month off. HISTORY OP THE WARRINGTON BRANCH. BRO. MAYBURY'S PAPER. Bro. G. MAYBURY, P.D.C.R., read a brief history of the Warrington district. He said : This district is evidently an old one. I find that it came into existence about the year 1831. In 1834 there were 358 courts in connection with the Royal Order of Foresters' and two courts evidently belonged to Warrington. Through the arbitrary measure of the supreme officers in 1831, a disruption was caused among the members of the Royal Order. This district attended the Manchester Convert- tion and severed its connection with the Royals, slid joined in the formation of the present Ancient Order. The members who belonged and formed this district were very enthusiastic for the well being of their fellow men.We find in the first directory of the order published that the Warrington andKnutsford district was comprised of eight courts (we do not find any reference to Kurd s- ford in the directory), while this district has six courts belonging to the good old order to-day. The men who formed this district had the grit and pluck so well known to exist among Englishmen for we find that in 1840 (nine years after the formation of this district), they had the honour of forming the Executive Council and of hold- ing in this good old town the seventh High Court. The Warrington Executive proved one of the most success- Ml up to that time, for during the first quarter of its existence it issued no less than 100 dispensarions for the opening of new courts.
